On motion of Hon. Geo. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting the construction of Canadian National Railway lines, and to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may provide for the construction and completion by the Canadian National Railway Company (hereinafter called "the
C.N.R.-Construction

Company") of the lines of railway mentioned or referred to in the schedule to these resolutions (hereinafter called "the said lines of railway");
2.	That any of the said lines of railway connecting with the Canadian Government Railways may be declared by the Governor in Council to form part of the Canadian Government Railways. Lines of railway so declared (hereinafter called "Government Railway lines") shall be constructed by the company on behalf of His Majesty and the company shall cause the title to the necessary lands or interests in lands to be acquired in the name of His Majesty.
3.	That with respect to Government Railway lines the Governor in Council may authorize advances to be made to the company from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to cover the necessary expenditure in acquiring such lands or interests in lands and in constructing and completing such lines of railway.
4.	That with respect to the lines of railway mentioned or referred to in the said schedule' other than Government Railway lines (which other lines are hereinafter referred to as "National Railway lines") the Governor in Council may authorize the guarantee of the principal and interest of the securities of the company issued under the provisions (save as herein varied) of section 26 of chapter 13 of the statutes of 1919, to an amount approved by the Governor in Council but not exceeding $40,000 per mile of such National Railway lines.
5. That the certificate of the minister as to the mileage of the National Railway lines shall for these purposes be conclusive, but the minister may issue interim certificates from time to time based upon the estimated mileage and a final certificate to accord with the miles and fractions of miles actually constructed, each line of railway being treated as a separate line.
6.	That the mileage of the said lines of railway and the cost of construction thereof mentioned in the schedule hereto shall be deemed to be merely estimated distances and costs.
7. That the nature and form of securities to be issued and guaranteed shall be approved by the Governor in Council and signed by the Minister of Finance, and may, as the Governor in Council decides, be secured by mortgage or deed of trust.
8.	That to enable the work of construction and completion of the National Railway lines to proceed forthwith the Governor in Council, pending the issue and disposal of such guaranteed securities, may authorize advances to be made to the company from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, such advances to be reimbursed to His Majesty by the company from the proceeds of the sale or disposition of such guaranteed securities.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.
On clause 1:

I wish to make an explanation. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No objection.

I do not desire to object to proceeding with the resolution, but I wish to draw the attention of the government, and the Minister of Railways more especially, to the fact that they are going into an expenditure of about $25,000,000 for the construction of branch lines. I scanned the resolution very rapidly, and I observed that 71 miles are located in Nova Scotia, 25 miles in New Brunswick, 14 miles in Quebec, and 29 miles in Ontario, and all the rest goes to the west. I do not object that the proposal be adopted. I have had the honour of representing my constituency for twenty-five years, and his Honour the Speaker (Mr. Lemieux) has represented Gaspe, the adjoining constituency, for a longer period. We have on several occasions called the attention of governments in the past to the singular position in which the people of the Gaspe peninsula are situated. In twelve years from now the four-hundredth anniversary of the landing of Jacques Cartier on Canadian soil will occur in this the oldest-inhabited part of Canada. And we are still asking for a decent railway service. When Sir Wilfred Laurier took office in 1896, one hundred miles of railway had been built, as far as New Carlisle, following out a proposal made to the parliament of that day by Sir Hector Langevin and Sir Charles Tup-per in 1882. Sir Hector Langevin at that time was Minister of Public Works and leader in the province of Quebec, Sir Charles Tupper was Minister of Railways. In 1882, parliament voted an amount for the construction of this branch of the Intercolonial railway from Matapedia towards Gaspe Basin. This undertaking was handed over to a private company, and the misfortunes of that district began with that date. Sir Wilfred Laurier took office in 1896, and the present Speaker of this House asked, very fairly for his constituency-because at that time Gaspe was the only constituency in Quebec which

C .N.R .-Construction
had no railway service whatever-that the line should be continued from New Carlisle to Gaspe. The remaining one hundred miles were completed, making in all two hundred miles of railway. The late Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) had a law passed through this House by which any two hundred miles of railway connecting with the Intercolonial or with government-owned railways might be merged into the Canadian National system. We have urged this for many years without success. The present two hundred miles of railway line are owned by two companies, the shareholders of which reside in England. They give service merely to keep the railway alive, and the result is that that part of Quebec, which is the most interesting from its maritime aspect, from its valuable resources, from the attractiveness of its territory and from its very energetic population, has remained to this date the most poorly served part of Canada in the matter of railways. It seems strange to these people, inhabiting the oldest part of Canada, while we are voting millions for new parts of Canada which are barely settled at the present time, or which are yet to be settled by newcomers to this country whom we welcome

that the oldest settlers, the people of the oldest part of Canada, should remain still without any adequate railway service.
Lately we have called the attention of Sir Henry Thornton to this state of affairs. Sir Henry Thornton volunteered to have an inspection made of these lines and to have them operated as if they were the property of the Dominion, as branch lines of the Intercolonial railway, because they are de facto branch lines of that road. The two counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure are inhabited by 60,000 people, and we could easily have three times that population if we had a proper railway service. These two constituencies cover 10,000 square miles of the most fertile territory in the province of Quebec, with a double advantage of being situated by the sea, having thousands of miles of timber and pulpwood, mineral resources, fertile soil, and splendid fisheries producing some of the finest fish of the North American continent. Our rivers are visited yearly by the cream of American and Canadian society, from His Excellency down, and that has been the case for the last forty years. A member of the Royal House has gone to the extent of establishing a residence at New Richmond to take advantage of the fisheries in these attractive regions. Nevertheless the district has remained in a quiescent state. During the first ten years that I had the honour
of representing the constituency in this House, the population increased in one county alone by 5,000. During the next decade, from 1911 to 1921, the population increased by only 500. Why? Because the industries in both Gaspe and Bonaventure, one after another moved away across the Baie des Chaleurs to the Intercolonial where they could get service over which they could send their produce. At Nouvelle, to begin with, the Province of Quebec Lumber Association transferred all its lumber over to Dal-housie, and it is operating on the main line of the Intercolonial. The same thing happened at Bonaventure and New Richmond where the mills of the McLean Lumber Corporation were transferred to Bathurst, and to-day we witness the spectacle of this lumber being cut in these two countries and being transported in booms across the Baie des Chaleurs, a distance ranging from 25 to 50 miles to be sawn and placed on board cars to be exported to the Canadian and American markets at great disadvantage and loss. The result of this is that the young people are leaving these two counties daily, and settling, unfortunately a large number of them, in the United States. We are losing our population, and this because we have not an efficient railway service which would develop the resources of these two constituencies as they should be developed. I know the Minister of Railways or the government has handed over the operation of the Canadian National Railways to a board of directors. Sir Henry Thornton ia willing to operate these lines as branches of the Intercolonial. We find ourselves in presence of these two companies holding these roads for a price, and between the two the people are not getting the service. There must be a solution to this, and I wish to attract the attention of the Minister of Railways and the government of Canada to this fact. Hon. Mr. Carvell and some of his associates on the Railway Commission visited the constituencies two or three years ago and made an elaborate report, which is now in the possession of the Minister of Railways, pointing out that these two constituencies did not have the railway service to which thev were entitled. And if an application were made to the Railway Commission to-morrow, I have no doubt that an order would be issued which would place these two Enelish companies in the position of having to give up the operation of these railways, because I understand their resources are not sufficient, to give the country the service to which it is entitled.
C.N.R.-Construction

We have on these two roads some very antiquated locomotives. We have no rolling stock whatever. The rolling stock that we have comes from other roads, and still every pound of freight and every passenger coming over these 200 miles of territory cannot reach any other railway than the Intercolonial. After the hon. the Speaker had succeeded in having the second hundred miles of this road completed, I had the honour of introducing in this House in 1904 a bill to authorize the contraction of the interprovincial railway bridge over the Restigouche river between Cross Point and Campbellton, the reason at that time being to link up these two railways with the Intercolonial Railway at Campbellton. We have now communication with Matapedia by which we can easily reach Montreal, Quebec, Ontario and the West. But our communication with the American market and with the Maritime provinces is defective. By the construction of this bridge over the Restigouche river between Quebec and New Brunswick, we would have an easy access to these railways, to the Intercolonial going east and west, to the International running from Campbellton to St. Leonards and the border of the state of Maine, where it would connect with the American system of railways and would place the entire Gaspe Peninsula within 24 hours of Boston, the great .fish market of the United States. .We have in the Baie des Chaleurs some of the most magnificent fish in the province. We have pulpwood galore. We have untold wealth in minerals. We have all these resources, but we need a much better railway service. Before the Minister of Railways proceeds much further with this railway legislation, I trust he will give this state of affairs his serious consideration. He will find in the archives of his department a very elaborate report issued last year by one of his officials, Mr. Fraser, who went down there and made a thorough investigation into the whole system. In this report Mr. Fraser points out that these 200 miles are the most valuable branch of the Intercolonial east of Montreal. Still they are inadequately unoperated, the people have not the service, and the Canadian National Railways are without the proceeds that would be derived from the proper operation of these roads. We have a huge deficit in connection with our Canadian National Railways and the only way in which that deficit can be reduced is by obtaining business for the system. Here is an excellent opportunity. People are willing to stay at home here and are anxious to develop the place. We find here large families, and the people are not 
troubled with any advanced hour or any eight-hour-a-day system, nor are they bothered with labour unions. They are of the old type of Canadians who inhabited this country years ago. This is an ideal country for the development of all our industries and, as I have observed, there are large families-families of ten, twelve and fifteen children are frequent. We have lately seen at Gaspe itself the creation of a new diocese, which in the province of Quebec means the centre of a large district; and the absorbing powers of the French-Canadian race are strikingly exemplified in the fact that the first Roman Catholic bishop of this diocese is the Right Rev. Monseigneur Ross, the descendant of a Scotsman, though a French-Canadian himself. This part of the province of Quebec has thus become the nucleus of a new district, and when the Minister of Railways is considering this development of the National Railway system generally he will find a very notable example of what has occurred in the Lake St. John district as well as in the Chicoutimi district in the fact that this part of the province of Quebec has been erected into a diocese with a bishop in charge. He will also see in the Three Rivers district a section of the country that is fast becoming the industrial centre of the whole of Canada.
I am in favour of immigration, and during the past twenty-five years I have voted for the expenditure of millions untold for this purpose, for the construction of railways, and for the advancement of Canada generally. But really I consider that this part of the province of Quebec has been overlooked; and when His Honour the Speaker and myself placed the matter before Sir Henry Thornton on a purely business basis he was amazed at the state of affairs that actually existed. To such an extent, indeed, did it appeal to him that he offered at once to undertake the operation of these railways as branch lines of 'the Intercolonial. But we are held up by these English companies who are keeping the roads alive merely for the purpose of obtaining their price. Now, there must be a solution for this condition of things, and I call upon the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), who is familiar with the province of Quebec, his colleague, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), and the government, to p-ovide this solution as soon as possible. We are not asking for the construction of railways; we are merely asking for the operation of a railway that has already been constructed, a portion of it forty years ago and the other portion within the last fifteen years. We simply want to give to the people the service to which they

C.N.R.-Cons true tion
are entitled; and that they are entitled to this service is admitted by the Railway Commission and all officials who have gone over the ground. I trust therefore that proper attention will be given tins matter before long and that the people of Gaspe peninsula will receive that consideration which they have a right to expect at the hands of the country.
Mr. HANSON; I am sure the Minister of Railways must have a heart of stone if he does not give heed to the eloquence of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. MarcilV While this subject is under consideration I want to call to his attention the position of a branch line of the Intercolonial railway.
Would the hon. member bo kind enough to allow me just a few more words beforp he proceeds?

I should rather like to continue; the topic I propose discussing is akin to the one just dealt with by my hon. friend. There is in the province of New Brunswick a line known as the Kent Northern railway, the only branch line in the province which has not been taken over by the Dominion. That line was included in the scheme projected by the Minister of Railways in the late government, and but for the attitude of the owners it would ere this have formed a part of the government railway system. I understand that the only difficulty in the old days was with regard to the price. The government at that time were willing to pay $60,000 for the twenty-eight miles of railway line, while the company that owned the property expected considerable more. It has lately come to my knowledge, however, that the company is now willing to sell at the offer originally made by the government, and I will ask that the Minister of Railways, while he is taking into consideration the appeal of the hon. member for Bonaventure. to give serious heed to the request of the people of the county of Kent in New Brunswick, that that line be taken over. During the recent very severe winter the people of that county, numbering some 25,000, were for forty-two days without railway communication. This is a great handicap to a part of the country, such as this is, that is well settled and is thriving industrially, besides being a considerable farming and fishing community. These people are entitled to a better service and the only possible means of providing such a service is for the government to take over this branch line. Again I ask the minister to take into earnest and serious consideration the question of acquiring that line.

While in opposition I took the opportunity on various occasions to call to the attention of the Minister of Railways the situation in regard to certain branch lines which were at that time needed in the county I have the honour to represent, the county of Charlevoix. These two branch lines extend respectively from Baie St. Paul to St. Urbain and from Murray Bay to Naim fall. The distance between St. Paul and St. Urbain is nine miles and the line would cost approximately $200,000. I had the assurance of the Minister of Railways at that time, Hon. J. D. Reid, that he would send his engineers to look over the site with a view to seeing whether something could not be done in the immediate future. This, I might observe, was in the year 1920, or perhaps in 1921. There is a great mine operated by the Titanium Ore Company in this district; and the General Electric Company of the United States, during the war, succes-fully operated a mine next to it. I have no doubt that if proper facilities were afforded by a branch line the people that now own the capital stock of the Titanium Ore Company, and who belong to the province of Quebec would be able to carry on operations that would prove of great benefit to that district. At St. Urbain there is a national park which the Department of the Interior has set aside as a special reserve for fishing and hunting, while there are a great number of clubs under the control of the provincial government in this locality. As in the case of the county which my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) represents a great number of visitors from various parts of Canada, as well as from the United States, and indeed, from other parts of the province of Quebec, pass through this district of which I am speaking, every year, spring, summer and fall, and I am sanguine that if this branch line were built it would increase that traffic and bring more money and people to the place. This district is also a great farming centre, from which butter, cheese and other products are shipped to other parts of the province of Quebec. Then there is the other branch line to which I have referred, from Murray Bay to Naim fall. It was constructed eleven years ago before the main line of the Saguenay railway was built. But up to the present time the government has not officially taken possession of it. The line has been leased for a nominal rental to a pulp company. I am informed that about $100,000 would put the line into proper shape. A great deal of cheese and butter
C.N.R.-Construction

is produced in this district and extensive lumbering operations are carried on, so that there is plenty of freight business for the railway. Although the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and the new board of directors of the Canadian National Railways have apparently overlooked the transportation requirements of my district, I hope that they will take the matter once more into consideration and do something. There is also the completion of the Quebec and Saguenay Railway, to Chicoutimi from Murray Bay, a distance of about 55 miles, which has to be undertaken in the very near future if the main railway is to be made to pay. The previous government was very free with assurances that in the very near future they would do something for these people, but apparently these were merely election promises. I hope the new government will do better than their predecessors. To this end, I would extend to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals another invitation to visit this district next July, when I am sure they will agree with me that Baie St. Paul and Murray Bay for scenic beauty are not equalled anywhere else in the Dominion-in fact they will be charmed with the delightful county of Charlevoix-Montmorency.

I can assure my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that the railway in Kent was looked after by those more closely concerned in the interests of the county long before he was politically born. If we have not control of the branch lines down there it is not the fault of the Conservative government; they made an offer to the provincial authorities, which offer was declined. I for one have done all I could with reference to the matter, without bringing it before the House as a complaint against any government, and to-day it is being looked after by this government in a way which I think will be for the advantage of my county.
I can assure my hon. friend that this business is in good hands and that we can get along fairly well without his interference.

Mr. Chairman, here is a very interesting situation for the Minister of Railways. The pathetic plea made by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has at least excited the sympathy of my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) because they have a fellow-feeling; they both have railways in their respective counties that have been built for forty years, operated by private companies during all that 4 p.m time, and now that these companies are unable to go on any longer my hon. friends want to dump the lines on to the 
government. They want to attach them to the 'National Railways, notwithstanding that my hon. friends from the province of Quebec are always complaining about our National Railway deficits. There is no hope of escaping these deficits-

If my hon. friend will allow me- does he know that in the province of Quebec we have the shortest railway mileage per thousand of population in the whole Dominion, and that our railways always show a surplus?
If there is a deficit on the National Railways it is not due to lack of traffic in the province of Ontario.
Nor in Quebec, either.
I do not think my hon. friends will deny that in the province of Quebec there is a strong sentiment against government ownership and operation of railways, and I base my remarks upon that fact.
If I might correct my hon. friend-the sentiment is much less strong since the new management took over the National Railways.

That is very interesting, Mr. Chairman, and, to me, very satisfactory. It has really been worth while to have a change in the management if it has resulted in removing the antipathy to government ownership and operation of railways that formerly existed in the province of Quebec. With the hon. gentleman's province in favour of public ownership, I think we may safely say that the whole Dominion is favourable. So I am very glad to hear from my hon. friend of this change of sentiment in his province. I have a good deal of sympathy for my hon. friend from Bonaventure with his two hundred miles of railway built forty years ago and still in the hands of a private company. We are told, mostly by the press of the province of Quebec, including the Montreal Gazette, that the only way to run railways is by private ownership. Yet here is a railway in the beautiful county of Gaspe, a county of fertile soil and rich in natural resources, where the traffic is so light that no private capital can be induced to continue the operation of this forty-year-old road. Therefore what private capital has thrown aside parliament is urged to transfer to our National Railways. I am not taking the position that some relief should not be given tc that beautiful county, but I just want to draw the attention of the House to the remarkable situation. Not only in the county

C.N.R.-Construction
of Gaspe, but down in the province of New Brunswick there is a line that excites sympathy.

The first
part of the line I referred to was built forty years ago, the other part at a later date Every year there is a surplus on the first hundred miles of between $50,000 and $60,000, but on the second hundred miles there is always a deficit; so one practically balances the other. What we are urging the government to do is merely to give service on these branch lines that they give on the other branch lines of the Intercolonial Railway. Last September although four hundred cars were required only forty were received in the district, and of course this means that business is being lost. I merely want Sir Henry Thornton to operate these lines as if they were branches of the Intercolonial Railway The Dominion has spent a million dollars in subsidies, for which no results are being obtained.

That is very interesting, too, but the fact still stands out that the private ownership of this railway has not been a success; and not being a success, my hon. friend turns to national ownership and wants the burden of this unsuccessful railway to be assumed by the National Railways.
Was it not the same in respect to our National Railways?-that their unsuccessful operation under private ownership prompted my hon. friends to try government ownership?

I see, Mr. Chairman, I have got myself into a lot of trouble in merely trying to elucidate a point which I thought it well to bring to the attention of the House. I may inform my hon. friend that it was the failure of private ownership, supported-unwisely supported, extravagantly supported-by the government of my hon. friends opposite which built the National T ranscontinental.

Who built the Grand
Trunk?

Who built the Grand
Trunk Pacific?
Not the government.
The Grand Trunk Pacific never would have been built but for the support and assistance given by the government of that day.
They all got support.

Yes. I admit that private ownership failed. But not in the province of Ontario; it was always profitable there. It was when we went out into the West and built thousands of miles of railway through a wilderness that private ownership failed, and this country had to face the alternative of handing over to private corporations anywhere from fifty million to one hundred million dollars a year or else take over their failing railways. There was nothing else to do, as I see it, but to take over the system. My hon. friend has drawn me a little away from the point I was making. I am not raising any particular objection to the pathetic plea of my hon. friend from Bonaventure, but I wanted to point out the change that has taken place when the men who have been condemning private ownership now turn to public ownership to escape the burden that private ownership will not carry.

Is there not a greater change in my hon. friend's attitude? He advocated public ownership when private ownership failed in his province and elsewhere, and he is now contending that we should not now carry out the same principle in respect to a railway in a province where the population per mile of railway is less than anywhere else in Canada. It is all very well to talk of public ownership in provinces where there is great density of population, but when it comes to assisting a certain branch line that cannot carry on by itself in the province of Quebec, where we have the smallest population per mile of railway, my hon. friend reverses1 his principles. He is opposed to the taking over of that railway by the National system, though he advocated the taking over of the railways in his own province and elsewhere that had failed under private ownership.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would like to draw
the attention of the members of the committee to the fact that this resolution deals with specific lines of railway, and the question whether public ownership or private ownership is the more profitable is really beyond the bounds of paragraph 1 and the schedule which forms a part of it.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend has made four speeches while I am on my feet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am simply informing the committee what I must rule in regard to this paragraph.

You will permit me to say, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend misrepresented my attitude absolutely. I thought
C.NJt.-C onstruc tion

I had taken pains to say that I was not opposing what my hon. friend from Bonaven-ture asked. I did not oppose that.

I did not understand you to
approve of it.
Perhaps I was not as clear as my hon. friend from Lotbiniere, but I tried to make it clear that I was not opposing it. I was drawing attention to this particular situation-
Must we understand that you approve of it?
The Chairman will be ruling you out of order.

May I ask my hon. friend a
question? Must we understand that my hon. friend is in favour of it?

I am in favour of this:
If the president of the National Railway says that this is something that ought to be done I think this parliament ought to listen with very careful attention and give fair consideration to his recommendation. The other fact to which I wish to draw attention-and I think I am within the rules in this, Mr. Chairman -is the generosity of the Minister of Railways towards our friends in western Canada. I think it was something like five million dollars that we voted for the Hudson Bay Railway. I find that this totals up an expenditure of $21,133,900 for railway extensions in western Canada.
It is a paying proposition.

It may be, but I doubt
very much if it will pay for some time. And even if it is a paying proposition I want to point out that the Minister of Railways is very generous in his treatment of the West. I \m not objecting to that.
It is good business.

But I say that our friends in western Canada ought to feel grateful for it. They ought to go home and tell their friends that this parliament of Canada representing the effete East as well as the West is not unsympathetic with the men who are growing grain on the prairies.

Not so
much so as the late government my hon. friend supported.

I think that is out of
order, Mr. Chairman.
You invited it,

Because if I attempted
to answer it I am afraid I should take all afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot prevent interjections if the hon. member does not object to them.

You know, Mr. Chairman, that I am not accustomed to wasting the time of the House, but I could make a defence of the late government particularly in its treatment of the West. I say that over $21,000,000 is to be spent for railway construction in western Canada, and if you include the Hudson Bay Railway it is nearly $27,000,000; and only $7,276,000 is to be spent in all the rest of Canada. I want my friends from the West to go home and tell their constituents that this parliament is just as anxious for the prosperity of the West as the men who are growing grain on the prairies, and we are proving it by voting this large sum for railway extensions in that part of the country. I do not object to the cost because I conclude-
May I ask a question? Does the hon. member realize that the city of Toronto will benefit more by the extension of these railway lines than the people living in the West?
No, I do not realize that at all, but I realize this, that of the money that will be spent in this direction the city of Toronto will pay more than any other part of the country.
Where do they get it?
What about Montreal?
Montreal will also contribute. Every large centre of population and of industry and wealth will pay its share.
Where do they get the wealth?

I might tell my hon. friend this, but I am afraid I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, that the city of Toronto and the city of Montreal were flourishing and prosperous before there was any West. Their prosperity may have been increased by the West.
You were only a camp of gypsies.
I think my hon. friend is out of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am trying to point out to my hon. friends from the West and to this

C.N.R.-Construction
House with what generosity they are being treated in the matter of railway construction. When they charge the constituency I represent with deriving the greater part of the profit from such extensions as this, I say that is not the case. The city of Toronto, the city of Montreal, and all the big cities in this country are the tax-paying centres of Canada.
Rats!

Somebody said "rats."
Look at the tax returns and especially the income tax and sales tax returns, the post office and custom house and all the rest of it, and what I say will be proven. This government derives its money, and its collection is made easy, because of the concentration of wealth in those cities.
What about that four hundred million bushels of wheat from the West?

That contributes a great deal to the prosperity of the railways, but it also contributes to the prosperity of the men who grow the wheat. My attitude in this House has always been, and is now, that the best thing that parliament can do for the West is to improve its transportation, and that is what we are doing. The only way you can get more money for your grain and obtain lower rates is to improve the railway and all other forms of transportation. I just rose for two purposes and I have been drawn over several different concession lines until I have diverted from those purposes. I wanted to point out to people interested in public ownership throughout this Dominion-not only in Ontario and the West, but also in the province which up to the present time has not been very sympathetic towards that policy-that the West is getting a tremendous railway expenditure of $27,000,000.
That was a business proposition, to the advantage of Canada, and the city of Toronto would benefit from this expenditure as well as the West.

That may be true, but I
wonder if my hon. friend disputes the logic of my statement. Are we spending $27,000,000 in the West or are we not?
We have not spent it yet.
Is that not what is proposed and are you not going to vote for it?
I am not in the witness box yet.

Then my hon. friend
does not know whether he is going to vote for it or not.
Indeed he does.

I venture the guess that
he will vote for it. Now, what I hope is that the members of this House who represent western constituencies-and I believe since they came here they have changed their viewpoint as to what the attitude of the East is towards the West-will tell their friends when they go home that there is nothing the parliament of Canada is more deeply interested in than contributing to the prosperity of the western part of this Dominion.

I only intend to speak for two or three minutes and I do not propose to say anything about public ownership as against private ownership other than this:	The people have before them to-day
evidence of the development of the Canadian National system, which is based on public ownership, and in which system they are the shareholders. If: you wish to see a further illustration of the success of public ownership look at the local street railway in Toronto and the development of power distribution in the province of Ontario. Then wait for the verdict of the people of the province in that respect on Monday next.
I want to deal with a matter of railway service which has apparently been ignored in the proposal before the House. In the province of Ontario it is proposed to spend nearly S2,000,000 on the Lac line which connects the Canadian Northern and the Transcontinental railway, and effects a great economy in the consumption of coal alone representing a saving of millions of capital. I thoroughly approve of the vote for this purpose and I am glad to see the item in the estimates.
It will improve transportation from the east to the west and from the west to the east.

It is in reality
a work for the general advantage of Canada and I am glad to see a vote for this purpose. I should also like to see the present management of the Canadian National Railways take up and carry out improvements in connection with their system at Toronto which would involve a comparatively small expenditure. Toronto believes in public ownership and supports it, and yet obstacles still exist to the complete unification of the government railways running into that city. The old Grand Trunk, the old Canadian Northern,
C.N.R.-Construction

and the "new National," as it is termed, have been consolidated. An evidence of that is given in the connection proposed with the Long Lac lines. But Toronto would like to see the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways entering that city under better conditions than now prevail. The two tracks entering the city by the east are four miles apart and the grades are over one per cent. Between the two tracks there was discovered some years ago a grade of one-half of one per cent which ought to be used. This could be done at very small expenditure, and I was under the impression there would have been provision made this year for that purpose. It would help to put the new station at Toronto, which represents an expenditure of four or five million dollars into use for it is not in use yet. The reason for the delay, I presume, is that the president and managing board of the National Railways have not yet prepared an estimate to lay before the government for the unification of the National lines running into Toronto. While an expenditure of four or five million dollars might be involved-perhaps a little more-the saving in the consumption of coal alone, in the overcoming of grades and the taking of a whole lot of traffic from the front of the city across town and farther to the north, would be so great, and would facilitate the economical handling of business to such an extent, that it would be worth, I imagine, three times the expense which may be involved. Therefore I would like to suggest to the minister-not that I hold him absolutely responsible for the administration of the National roads at the present time, seeing that the administration is now in the hands of the new president and his co-directors-the necessity of drawing the attention of the new management to that condition of affairs, and to ask for improvement there even though it necessitate a considerable expenditure. Because, as I have pointed out, the economies and benefits to be gained would more than compensate for the expenditure in question, I hope, therefore, the Minister of Railways will take an early opportunity of bringing to the attention of the board of management the statements I make here to-day. Probably the minister knows more about the situation - than the directors do because he is cognizant of what has occurred in the past. And there may be other parts of the country where similar improvements can be carried out. The unification of the system of railways that we have taken over has not been accomplished yet. There are a great many places where improvements like that proposed at Long Lac can be carried out at comparatively small expense and the 
great saving in the upkeep to say nothing of the improvement in the service would more than pay for the outlay in the course of three or four years. Unification is certainly most desirable in connection with the National railway system in the city of Toronto. At present there is an agitation going on rather to the discredit of the National system of railways. The public press are taking the matter up now and are wanting to know why the new union station-in reality it is not new it is five years old-has not been used. I hope the minister will draw the attention of the president and the board of management to this situation. Perhaps there will be an item in the supplementary estimates yet to be brought in that will make provision for this purpose. If that proves to be the case the government and the administration of the National road will be taking a still further step towards earning the appreciation of the people of the country.
As to what my hon. friend from Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) has said here to-day in regard to the local railway in his constituency -and I imagine that he is also expressing the views of the present Speaker (Mr. Le-mieux) in regard to the railway condition in Gaspe-the situation referred to ought to be cured. Perhaps it will be cured by the installation of gasoline engines capable of drawing passengers cars as well as freight cars. This will be a great advance in transportation in that district. I notice that the Canadian National Railway board is taking up that matter in various parts of Canada and perhaps relief may be found in that direction. While I do not want to interfere in any way with the freedom which has been given to the president and directorate of the National system in dealing with the railway question, I think no mistake is made in drawing the attention of the House, as well as the board of management, to the railway grievance that exists in Toronto and to the need for improvements which will effect a saving of hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in the maintenance charges, greatly assist the movement of traffic, help the development of Toronto, and make the investment we have made in these railways a striking success.
And this is all the more in favour of public ownership as against private ownership, and probably I have a right to bring it up now. I repeat what I said the other day, that company ownership has been an absolute failure in the United States. There is no provision for the recovery of the privately-owned companies and railways in the United States, except the intervention of the

C.N.R.-C onstruction
national government and the payment of immense subsidies to them for the reconstruction, electrification and re-equipment of the company-owned railways in that country. They have absolutely failed in the United States, the people there have no longer faith in them, and the only relief ahead of them, as far as I can see is public ownership. We shall hear the announcement in the speeches which will be made by President Harding when he goes to the people-as he intends to go to them on the railway question almost in the next few days-that private ownership has failed. The New York Central railway and the Pennsylvania railway have failed. They cannot finance for reconstruction, electrification, or re-equipment.
Referring to my hon. friends from Qudbec, I do not propose to say anything offensive to them, but I will compliment them on getting behind the movement for the nationalization of the railways and the improvemeuu of the railways in the direction of giving the people better transportation facilities, especially in connection with the waterways. We have not only to regulate the railways and take them over, but we have to find the money to improve the waterways, and at the same time we must regulate the steamships which now use these waterways to levy unjust charges upon the people who use their system.
Not Ontario.

-and the Maritime provinces.
I would ask the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), when he goes home at the end of the week, and probably makes a political speech, to quote these figures to his constituents. During the last ten years, from 1913 to the year 1920-23, the Public-Works department, or the government, have spent in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario the sum of 198,916,428 on public buildings, dredging, docks and so forth. In the three western provinces during that period they spent a total sum of $10,465,000. When I go to the west I am going to tell them that we are rather grateful to Sir Henry Thornton for the proposal to spend these large sums of money on the western Canadian roads.
I am also going to quote these figures of expenditures made in the East. No good purpose is ever served in this House, or on the hustings or anywhere else, by making such speeches as were made by my hon. friend from West Toronto in this House this afternoon.

I think some consideration should be given to the stand we are taking on this matter. This is a demand on parliament for the construction of branch railways to the extent of 1,000 miles, representing an expenditure about $25,000,000. Before the day is over I suppose there will be a demand from members of the House for an additional 1,000 miles of branch lines and an additional expenditure of $25,000,000. I may be permitted very frankly to state the awkward position in which some of us are placed concerning the management of the railways. This is another instance where we have a clash between control and responsibility. Speaking in Montreal some time ago before the Cartier Club, the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) stated that we on this side had abandoned our policy in railway matters to rally to his viewpoint, and that you could not point to a Liberal who would dare advocate private ownership. But on the estimates of the Minister of Marine (Mr. Lapointe) the leader of the Opposition took the opposite stand, and after vigorously setting forth his policy, stated that we were merely carrying out the scheme laid down by Mr. Ballantyne; and I suppose, after we have allowed this resolution to pass and approved of it, he will say that we lack consistency, and that events are bearing testimony to the excellency of his own policy as against ours. The hon. member for West Toronto only a minute ago tbok the.occasion of this resolution to raise once more the question of public and private ownership coming into conflict.
C .N.R.-Construction

Now, we have to deal with facts. The question now is not whether or not we should enter into a scheme of government ownership, but it is how best we can deal with the situation as it is and as we found it when we came into power in 1921. The choice is not to be made, it was made by hon. members opposite when they were in power, and it was the late government which loaded on this government the system that we have now to deal with. In opposition we said, and still say, at least I still say, that it was a mistake to acquire these roads on the conditions on which they were purchased, by accepting at par all the obligations and debts which these railways carried at the time. We said in opposition, and we also believe now, that it was a mistake for the late government to complete the ship programme of the late government, when it became evident that these ships might as well be burned or sunk, because they would be useless. But, as a matter of fact, we have the railways and we have the ships. The fact that we have resolved to submit them to a fair trial is no indication at all that we accept the principle against which we voted, or that we withdraw anything of the criticisms which we offered when these matters were first before parliament. It ill behooves the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) to sneer at the government now or at some of the Liberal members, when he more than any other is responsible for the present situation. We are now asked to add a number of miles of railway to this system.
What alternative had the country at the time the railways were taken over?
My point is: What alternative have we to-day?
I am asking what alternative there was when the railways were taken over.
I am not discussing that It was ruled that it was out of order.
Side-stepping.

I say that after we have decided to submit these railways to a fair trial, it is unfair for the leader of the Opposition to claim that we have abandoned our principle of private ownership. I will not discuss what alternative there was some years ago, because that is not the question here; I say that we haye no alternative now I will go further, I have no hesitation in saying that if we had an alternative, I for

one would favour at once the disposal of these railways to private ownership.
At what price?
One dollar.

I am afraid that the discussion has, perhaps, gone beyond these resolutions. I do not, however, object to anything that has been said, because I feel that the committee and members of parliament have a duty to perform. I think we could expedite the business of parliament if we could let these resolutions go through and get into the hands of every member the bill based on them with all the details. Then they would be prepared to discuss it, taking as much time as they like. I am not going to discuss government ownership, because we have it. We want to do the best possible in the circumstances, and the sentiment of the House seems to be in that direction.
The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has stated the case of the railway in which he is interested, and all he has said is true. Some years ago, the second portion of this railway was built, heavy subsidies, excess subsidies being paid on account of the many bridges, and the construction was very expensive. But of late, at least, the operation of that line has been anything but satisfactory. Sir Henry Ihemton, I think, had a conference with the president of that road, and he expressed a willingness, on terms, to take over the operation, but up to the present time no arrangement has been arrived at. I agree that there ought to be some way, particularly as regards a line that was largely built by the government, by which the people in the district who depend upon that line might get some service.
The thing that appealed to me in the remarks of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), was the invitation to come down. I understand the situation in which the lines that he spoke of are placed. I assure him that I will bring his remarks to the attention of Sir Henry Thornton and the board. I might point out that in these resolutions there is not a single line that has not been recommended by the Board of Directors of the Canadian National Railways.
Do all the lines included in these resolutions connect with government-owned railway lines?

These lines are divided into two classes. Those of one class are called government railways, including the old government line. These are dealt with separately in these resolutions. Then these other lines that are proposed will become branches of the Canadian National system. As to the county of Kent, New Brunswick, the Kent Northern railway is twenty-seven miles long, and I quite appreciate the fact that it might just as well have been twenty-seven inches long so far as its operation has been of any practical value. The question has been discussed as to how these people can best be served in that section of the country, because they are not served now. An effort was made by the previous government to take over the Kent Northern, and large petitions have come in from the county of Kent asking that the Moncton-Buctouche line be extended 18 miles to serve a greater number of people outside of the town of Richibucto, or Rexton, I believe, through which it passes. These matters are under consideration, and I have asked the management of the Canadian National Railways, as soon as they can possibly
C.N.R.-Construction

do so, to make a thorough investigation of the situation in the county of Kent, because my hon. friend behind me (Mr. Leger) has made my life miserable for the past three months over the question and will continue to do so, I am afraid, if I do not do something. However, I am awaiting reports from the Canadian National board. Under the Branch Lines Act lines connecting with the government railways can be dealt with, but any bargains made must be approved by parliament.
The question of the Inverness railway has also come before the Canadian National board, and so far as I can ascertain from previous reports, the people of that section are not being served by that railway. It was owned by a coal company; and while I must not say harsh things, it has b.een represented to me, nevertheless, with some fair show of credibility, as I think, that, like some of the big railways in the United States, this company has squeezed out any other that tried to do business because it gave all its traffic to the railway it owned itself. This is the situation in regard to the Inverness railway and it is possible that something practical may be done in the matter before another session of parliament.
With regard to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), I like that hon. gentleman because he keeps good-natured every day, except on the Twelfth of July, and he is always a strong advocate of public ownership; in fact he could not get elected in the city of Toronto if he were not. But he made this mistake, though not intentionally, that the programme will only extend over three years, the amount of money he suggested for the whole project being some $27,000,000 or $28,000,000. So that for the present year the appropriation would be one-third of that.
There are some lines that ought to be completed, such as, for instance, the Long Lac line.

That is under construction now. As to the Hudson Bay railway, nothing has been voted yet, so that the hon. gentleman was in error in that regard. There was a small vote, but it was for the purpose of protecting works that we have there now. I might intimate to the committee, however, that believing that the promises of the government and of parliament should be carried out, I shall consider putting a certain amount in the Supplementary Estimates in this connection. Now, my hon. friend from East York-is it? or South York? I do not know which, for they have changed the designation of the constituencies since I used to campaign

against him (Mr. Maclean)-suggests amalgamating these lines at once. Towns and villages have sprung up outside Toronto, and they need railway accommodation. You cannot very easily or quickly make any change in that respect, however. The question of grading has something to do with it. The old Grand Trunk tried to get a better grade from Scarborough Heights into Toronto, but they discovered that to go by the lake front would raise a riot, and my hon. friend's paper kicked up a fuss about it.
What was needed was a real scheme.

There was another scheme my hon. friend suggested, but it would cost a great deal of money. However, these things will no doubt be accomplished in time. At present the board is endeavouring to uniform the whole system as expeditiously as possible, and so far as this is concerned there is no difference in opinion as regards east or west, north or south. What I have submitted is the Canadian National board's programme, as handed to me, and which I think is a good thing for the railways and for the country generally. One of the reasons for this three-year programme being placed on the statutes is that the people may understand exactly what they are going to get for some time. It has been stated, and quite properly so, that the psychology of those who advocate a thing has a great deal to do with influencing its promotion. Many of these branch lines in the West are not new structures; very many miles of these lines have been graded, some of the grades having been constructed since the war, although the rails have not been laid down. There are some four hundred miles of grading already done, and all we propose to do is to lay the rails. Surely, no one would suggest that it is bad business, if after investigation the previous board decided to build these lines, for the present board to complete the work. It will be a good investment for the company and for the country as well. If the committee will agree to my suggestion and let us get this matter embodied in a bill I think it will expedite our business. Every member will have the bill before him and we shall bring it up on Monday in order to discuss the details.
I will comply with the request of the minister and defer my remarks until the bill is distributed.

In view of the minister's
request, I do not want to enter into any discussion of this matter now, but I want to know whether he can give us any information

C.N.R.-Construction
as to why a certain branch line in the province of Alberta has been eliminated from this schedule. The line to which I refer is known as the Bruederheim railway. In the month of March the Alberta members, realizing that Sir Henry Thornton is a very busy man, got together and decided that one meeting with him should be made to cover all the various points which they desired to submit to him. We all had railway troubles in our constituencies, and we laid our grievances before Sir Henry Thornton, who presented to us a schedule which I understood at the time-as I think other hon. members from Alberta will bear me out-was practically along the same line as that which we have before us to-day. In that schedule was this proposed railway commencing at the town of Bruederheim and extending easterly for a distance of 31 miles. The people have been asking for this railway for a number of years, and they had the assurance of Sir Henry Thornton that it would be undertaken; at least it was in the schedule, which was submitted to the delegation and all it required was the attention of parliament. But before going any further, some few *weeks later, he being out of town, I telephoned to the deputy minister. He was i)ot in at the time, so I asked the gentleman who answered the telephone to ascertain if it was correct that the schedule which had been presented to me by Sir Henry Thornton was O.K.. A couple of hours later he telephoned me that my information was correct. Naturally, I am very much disappointed to find that this line is omitted from the schedule to the resolution. If this is an oversight, I hope that before the minister brings down the bill he will make good the omission.

I wish to confirm the
remarks of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Lucas). The line he mentions is very, very badly needed. I understand it was promised about twenty years ago to the people in the country through which it will run. In my own constituency men are hauling their grain to the railroad for distances up to thirty miles, and this, as 5 p.m. is well known, is such a severe handicap that they cannot possibly carry on their farming at a profit. On account of the continued failure to build this line many people have left the district, and the only way in which we can induce those who are still there to remain, and can also encourage new settlers, is to construct this railway without further delay. I sincerely hope therefore that there is an oversight in not including this line in the schedule of proposed branch line construction; and, if so, that it will be included at an early date.

Mr. Chairman, it is a real pleasure to rise and express my appreciation for the happy thought the government has had in extending into the county of Labelle, one of the main branches of the National Railways. Indeed, in this proposed measure before the House we note that fourteen miles have been added to the National Railways in the province of Quebec. These fourteen miles, I am happy to say, lend themselves for the most part to the development of this important branch which projects from the main line, near Montreal, and penetrating into the region of the Laur-entides extends to the county of Labelle.
I therefore wish to express my thanks and those of my electors to the government for having realized this important work, of extending this railway. In fact, twelve of the fourteen miles will be built for the purpose of connecting the main line from Montreal to Ottawa at a place known as Freniere with another point called Rinfret Junction which is the beginning point of the railway known as Montfort, and which has existed for a great number of years in that region. These twelve miles of rail will therefore be built in such a way as to link up the Montfort railway with the National main line from Montreal to Ottawa. This connection is very important; it is absolutely necessary and will contribute in making of this branch line one of the important lines of the province of Quebec. I especially wish to thank the government for having completed the branch line of the Montfort railway which was later on acquired by the Canadian Pacific Railway and finally was included in our national system of railways. This completed work comprises the construction of about two miles of railway, from a point called China Clay extending to the village of St. Remi d'Amherst which is situated close to the centre of the county of Labelle. These two miles of rail were only laid down so as to complete the main branch line. In fact, for a great number of years, the railway existed up to the village of Huberdeau, situated on the borders of the county of Argenteuil. Later, so as to help the mining industry, the rails were extended about nine miles into the county of Labelle, on the borders of the townships of Ponsonby and Amherst; however, this extension covering nine miles was simply built for the transportation of freight and the products of the mine. Heretofore passenger trains had not been in circulation as far as that point. For ever so long the people of Labelle have

petitioned the government. I had the pleasure to accompany their delegations to request the late government to finish this work by building these few miles which were absolutely necessary to connect this railway with those southern settled districts of the county of Labelle. As a result of these steps, I am glad to see that the Liberal government has generously acceded to the request of the electors of my county and that in the proposed measure there is an item of $65,000 for the construction of these two miles of railway which will extend the National Railway up to the village of Saint Remi d'Amherst and which, later on I hope, will be followed by a further extension, as conditions render this work indispensable and which, I again state, will make of this line one of the most important branches of the National Railways in the province of Quebec. By thus establishing, through this branch line, its terminus at St. Remi d'Amherst, the National Railway Company comes to the rescue of the parishes which are settled in that region for a great number of years. The government desires to help colonization, this so important work, a truly national effort, that we propose to develop in the province and especially in the district of Labelle. The government assures itself, by linking these parishes, of an increase in traffic which will, I am sure, make of this line one of the most paying propositions of the National Railways.
The question of the National Railways is certainly one of the most important problems of the day. Since the beginning of this debate the subject has been dealt with most ably by the members who have preceded me. It is absolutely important, in a young country like ours, to further the work in connection with our railways. It is in settlements like those we have in the province of Quebec that we note the immense progress accomplished thanks to railway construction. I have but to point out, as an example, the north west of Montreal the beautiful region of Labelle, which was opened up by the Canadian Pacific Radway. This region like the one still older found in Gaspe, has now its diocese, it is inhabited by numerous and intelligent settlers who have made the heart of the Laurentian hills like a new province. It is due to the development of railways that this region has been settled -the work shall be carried on, I know, by the Canadian Pacific Railway, for I have their promise, as far as the distant valley of the Lievre, to the north of Mont Laurier, in the parishes of Ferme-Neuve and Sainte-Anne du Lac-and we will witness great strides in colonization in that part of the

province which is so dear to us. The sam: thing is being enacted in the centre of tha county of Labelle, and it is thanks to th: work done by the government through the extension of this line of the Canadian National Railway, as far as Saint-Remi d'Amherst that the settlers may rejoice in having new means to develop that part of the country. Numerous and rich mining industries are already established at Saint-Rem. d'Amherst, the farming industry has been progressing in that place for many years and this parish is surrounded by other flourishing parishes situated in the heart of Labelle county, which, at present, is at a distance of 20 to 40 miles from the northern system of the Canadian Pacific railway, and which now is directly connected, through this branch line of the Canadian National Railway, with the metropolis of Canada.
By opening up the colonization region of the county of Labelle the government insures the progress of the National Railways, because as it was pointed out with a great deal of truth, probably the chief cause of the deficits of our railways rests in the fact that we own, up to the present, great transcontinentals. only, which however, were necessary at the time of their construction. These branch lines which will extend to the northern parts of our province, to the extreme limits of settlements, and will afford us the advantage of opening up new districts to settlers, will also afford us the means of considerably increasing the traffic of our railways, owing to our rich natural resources which are unlimited in the northern parts of our province. Thereby, I say, will the government ensure the successful operation of our National Railways. We congratulate them and I heartily thank them both in my name and that of the electors of the county of Labelle, for the happy thought they had in developing the National railway and extending it as far as Saint-Remi d'Amherst.
I would ask the minister if provision will be made this session for a railway survey between Grande Prairie and the Canadian National Railway?

My hon. friend has heard me being chastised a few moments ago for disclosing arrangements prematurely. I shall have to follow the lines of the Minister of Finance and say, "Wait and see."
In regard to the other matter, I might say that perhaps a hundred lines are being pressed on the board, and as my hon. friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) said in reference to the amendment to the act providing for the

Dominion Lands Act
indemnities, I told them to take it back and clarify it. We can only spend so much money, and the clarified list is the one I have here now. It will take some years to get around to the point where we would have been had there been no war, but if members will be patient, as fast as the Canadian National Railway board can see its way clear after investigation to recommend further construction, the government, so far as the finances of the country will warrant, will meet the situation. The Canadian National Railway board had a much larger list for consideration, but on account of the financial situation they were asked to "clarify" it, and this is the "clarified" list.

There is one point that I think has not been brought to the attention of the House as to these western lines. I think I am correct when I say that there is not a single new line under contemplation here. They all represent, as I understand it, the continuation of work that was started before the war; they are rounding out the system-connecting up all the loose ends, as it were. Now these loose ends having been laid out, located, and in some cases work commenced upon them, the territory along these lines has been filled up with settlers. They have been waiting there for years, and the completion of these lines will mean an immediate increase in the tonnage of the various roads. This is not new construction. It is not like starting out to build a new line somewhere, but is simply carrying out the plans that were agreed upon and the finishing of work that was interrupted by the war. I would ask the minister if I am not correct in that.
I think my hon. friend is in the main correct. His remarks might not apply to every case, but practically they cover the case.

I would ask the minister when the bill comes up on Monday, if that is the day set, to bring down as much definite information as possible in regard to No. 19, the Dunblane branch to Mawer, Saskatchewan, about which I spoke to him last night. I have received further telegrams to-day asking that from the standpoint of economy the existing line up to the river be utilized as far as possible. It was pointed out to me to-day that if the line was to be built as proposed it would open up no new territory and bring no more traffic to the Canadian National line, but would involve the construction of about thirty miles of new road. We have a road already existing in that territory, and if
the minister could see fit to utilize this existing line as far as the river it would give a more direct connection and be more economical. An expensive dam was built on the river about a year and a half ago; if is a divisional point and within eight miles of the Beachy line, and I can see no reason why the connection across the river should not be made as direct as possible, unless it is that there are insurmountable difficulties in the way of bridging the river at Riverhurst. I would ask the minister to bring down all the information when this matter next comes up.
I expect that when the bill comes up next I shall have to have here with me one or two railway men from the head office in Montreal.

Before paragraph l of the resolution, which I believe embodies the schedule, carries, I would point out to Ihe minister the need for a correction in the spelling of one wo*d in Item No. 15 of the schedule. It says the "Eaton Branch." There was some years ago a town a few stations west of Eston called Eaton, and there was such a mix-up in mails that it became necessary to change the name of Eaton to Eaton ia. The word here should be Eston, not Eaton, and I would suggest that the correction be made in the bill.

On section 3-Issue of patent after death of applicant.
I think it would be better if the minister, as we take up each clause, were to give reasons for the amendments and changes proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Section 3
provides that when a homesteader dies before completing the duties necessary to earn patent, his legal representatives are excused from doing any further residence duty. The act as it stands calls for the erection of a house and the completion of cultivation, but as no further residence is required it is considered unnecessary to insist on the erection of the house, it being frequently the case that a house so erected will deteriorate in value before the estate could secure the opportunity of disposing of the land.
