On section 6-Terms of payment for school lands.

In connection with ihis clause, I notice that the provision for selling applies after the first day of January, 1923, the purchase price being divided into twenty equal amounts. I was wondering if the department is going to do anything to relieve the settlers who have purchased school lands under the old agreement. There are a great many settlers with whom I am acquainted who have purchased school lands on the old conditions providing for payment in ten years and have made payment of one-tenth of the purchase price. Some of them have improved that land, brought it all under cultivation, built houses and bams, and put down wells. A purchaser has such a place as this home but he has been unable to make, possibly, any further payment or, if any, only a very small one, and the interest has been accumulating. Now, I have had correspondence from several to the effect that they are unable to pay the principal and unable to meet even the interest, and in different cases they have

Dominion Lands Act
requested that some concessions be made to them to enable them to carry on. I believe, generally speaking, they are quite willing to pay the original purchase price, but in some cases they ask that the interest be deleted from the agreement. In view of the fact that a special concession is to be made for all new purchasers would it not be consistent that some concession should also be made for the old purchasers who have been struggling along for several years, who are good settlers, and who are anxious and willing to make good if given a chance. Has the minister any plan in view that is likely to be adopted for relief in such cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might point out to the hon. member that, in the position we occupy, our trusteeship is of rather a limited character. The provinces are consulted as to the areas that shall be sold and as to the terms upon which the lands shall be sold. They were consulted in this instance as to an extension of the periods over which payment of principal might be made. This matter came up in the discussion. The amendment as outlined by my hon. friend makes the period for the payment of principal twenty years instead of ten years, as under the old provision. The provinces agreed to this. Indeed, it is at their request, because they think the land will bring a greater price than it would under the old provision. The question of making it retroactive is a little difficult ; but as we are acting as a trustee we can be lenient in the collection of the principal. I think many of the contracts that are outstanding to-day will run twenty years. We have not pressed for payment of principal. Very frequently there are large delayed payments of interest; but if the cultivation is going on we do not press for payment. Sc that, without touching the contract in existence, the party who has the land under contract may run for fifteen or twenty years before he has finally paid up his principal.

In regard to the interest charged on the amounts overdue, a few years ago a regulation was issued charging 7 per cent on agreements entered into at 5 per cent on payments that were overdue. Is that still the policy of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, that
still stands. That also was an arrangement with the provinces.

I am not fully satisfied with the explanation, because this morning I received a letter from one of my constituents who was on the land referred to, and ho enclosed a letter which he received
from the department, which pointed out very clearly and explicitly that he was in arrears several years on his contract for principal and interest, and that unless he showed very good and sufficient reason in the near future why he should be carried any longer, without paying up some of the arrears, the contract would be immediately cancelled. That is the kind of thing the settler is up against. He is in constant fear of having his contract cancelled, unless he appeals to the department for special extensions of one year at a time. In view of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway, as I believe, has written up all its own contracts for a long period of time, to give settlers a chance, I would think it almost incumbent on the department to do likewise. Will the minister state if it is within the jurisdiction of the department to do this, without first getting the consent of the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think we could do it without consent, but I do not think it would be wise for us to do it without consultation and consent. So far it has not been done. We have kept the provinces fully informed of any suggested changes, and usually the changes have been suggested by the provinces themselves. The difficulty in the case the hon. member mentions is not particularly the arrears of principal, but the failure to pay interest. We do not wish to be hard on any one but as trustee for the province, without being unduly harsh and without creating hardship, we will have to try to collect the interest. That is one of the very serious complaints. I could produce innumerable letters, particularly from the departments of education of the prairie provinces, complaining bitterly that we are neglecting the collection of the interest payments due on these school lands sales. In the case of Alberta, I think the ordinary amounts of interest payments received this year by the province have fallen off over $100,000, and the province is largely, though not altogether, dependent upon that fund for carrying on its schools. It is of very real assistance to it in carying on its school work, and the pressure comes from the province to collect the interest. The provinces are not vitally interested in the collection of principal, because if they are receiving the interest the principal is a trust fund for that purpose anyway. They do insist on our trying to collect the interest, and while we are not desirous of creating haMshio yet we look upon it as a duty to try to collect, as far as possible, the interest which has accrued on these sales.
Dominion Lands Act

Has the question of
making the amendment retroactive been discussed with the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I
thought I mentioned that. It was discussed at the time we discussed the extensions, but it was felt, inasmuch as we did not press for principal payments that no great harm was being done. It would not make any change in the situation. It might, to some extent of course, relieve, if that were possible the payment of the 7 per cent, or the 1 per cent additional, on money that was overdue; but that would be a somewhat involved process, because of the difficulty that probably six per cent of the people under contract have paid. Clearly the only relief that could be given would be to those who did not pay; and it would be discrimination against those who did pay, so that it presents a somewhat difficult problem.

In that point of view, I would like to support the contention of the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) , not in regard to the department making no effort to recover the interest-I quite see the position in that respect-but in reference to making the amendment dealing with the payment of interest retroactive; because, while I recognize that the department has in very few cases pressed for the payment of the principal, at the same time I think it would tend to reassure the purchasers that the principal payments which they were expected to make from year to year would be reduced by that amount. I believe the precedent set by the Canadian Pacific Railway is a sound one in that respect. I believe the precedent set in our amendment to the Soldiers' Settlement Act was in the same direction; that is to re-assure these people that year by year the payments would not be greater than they could reasonably be expected to meet. Although pressure is not being exerted, I do think the moral assurance to the men in knowing that they could take advantage of this provision, and that they would not be expected to pay the principal, would have a beneficial effect. A good many cases have been brought to my notice, and I mentioned to the people concerned that I thought an amendment to this effect would be brought down in the bill which would be introduced, and that there would probably be an extension of time for payment of principal. I hope the minister will see his way to make the bill retroactive in that respect, thus affording the men who have already purchased and are in difficulty the

same opportunity of extending the payments as will be afforded under the new act.
Would the minister state what is the practice of the department in reference to the school lands which were sold and afterwards abandoned? Some of them were broken up and a good many were abandoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
So far as
possible we tried to lease them. There was a suggstion-if not a suggestion, a complaint-I think from the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) with respect to the number of sales that have taken place in recent years where prices were very high, running well over $50 per acre for raw land. Those people who have contracted to pay that price, find themselves in serious difficulties. He was asking if some relief could not be afforded in those cases. That is a very difficult matter, and I do not know how to get around it unless we do this: Where an individual, under a contract of sale, finds himself in difficulties, we lease to him, indeed we are glad to lease to him if he surrenders his contract, and then on the next occasion when the sale comes around, if the lands do not sell for the prices they did formerly, he can become a purchaser under the new contract. In the meantime he can be a tenant until such time as it is deemed advisable to re-sell the land. But of course we try in every case, if possible, to lease the land and to keep it from getting dirty and weedy.

When the sale of theoc iands is completed and the money as I understand, is turned in to the Dominion government, do you still continue to pay a rate of interest to the schools on that money for the benefit of the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are
simply trustees in the matter. We turn over such money as we collect, less cost of collection only, to the provinces, for them to distribute to the school districts of the provinces. They, in turn, distribute it.

Is the
money derived from the sale not turned in to the Dominion government?
Mr. STEWART. (Argenteuil): Yes, we are trustees, the money comes to the Dominion government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. We
simply turn over such interest as we collect. The trust fund itself is an interest bearing fund, of course, and the interest is turned over to the provinces as well. The trust fund is in the hands of the Dominion government.

1 have in mind a certain
district in my part of the country where a sale of school lands took place some years ago, and the residents, because of that, formed themselves into a school district. Some of the lands were abandoned later on, and I believe the secretary-treasurers1 of the districts have endeavoured to collect taxes on these lands from the Dominion government. When I took the question up with the department, the advice which I received was that they did not feel bound to pay the taxes to the school districts. I merely call to the minister's attention the circumstance that the school districts thus formed are in a very precarious position because of those abandoned lands, and because the government does not assume the responsibility of paying school taxes. I have particularly in mind an area in the Moose mountain country, districts that were opened up in 1916, the lands1 being sold in 1917.
Mr. SPEAKMAN1 Would the minister take the question of making this amendment retroactive very seriously into his consideration during the recess, take it up with the provinces further and, if they are agreeable, bring down an amendment to the legislation? Because I believe this would be a great benefit, would lift a certain load, and would give an amount of moral reassurance to the men who purchased under the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Inasmuch
as we hope to get through shortly, I was going to suggest that I would be very glad to take this matter up with the provinces during the recess. There will be no pressure during the year, and if the provinces are agreeable, the matter is1 immaterial to the department.
That was my idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It was felt
that really no hardship would result unless the Dominion government pressed for payment of principal on those lands. If we pressed for payment of principal money, of course there would be a very serious hardship; but so long as the provinces were content to allow extensions to be granted, provided, of course, that the interest or reasonable amounts of interest were being paid, then the individual holding the contract would suffer no great hardship. That was the feeling, I may say, when we discussed the matter before. But I will undertake to
take it up again with the provincial representatives and to present the views of members of the committee on the matter.

I am very glad, because I feel that although no actual hardship may be suffered, except by reason of the accrued interest, still there is a certain amount of hardship in feeling that heavy payments are impending, when they know that they will not be able to meet them; that they must apply for an extension year after year with the certainty that they will not be able to pay the principal.
The minister has not replied in regard to the point that I brought up.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is back to the vexed question of Crown lands paying taxes. So far as possible, we insist on the tenant, where land is leased, paying the ordinary taxes of the municipality; but where land is unoccupied, held by the Crown, I could not enlarge on what I have already said in respect to the matter.

I do not think I have had any requests from a municipal point of view. The requests have been merely from the school districts themselves. These lands are unoccupied. There was another question which I have mentioned a couple of times. I believe, during the session. It is prompted also by correspondence which I have received from people who, in former years, have bought school lands, that is, 'who have made a contract with the Dominion government to pay principal and interest based on a rate of interest of 5 per cent. I myself was one of the guilty parties in the year 1916. The minister knows, and the committee is well aware of the fact that we have visitations of hail, grasshoppers, drouth and various other things, which oblige people to defer interest or principal payments. I believe an order in council was passed by the former minister, which penalized the people by raising the rate of interest to 7 per cent. That was quite a hardship on people residing in the West, and I have received several protests from people who were under that disability. They have asked me to present their case in order to see if some concession could not be made, if the interest rate could not remain as it was before to all bona fide purchasers who are keeping up their payments, so that no penalty, by way of an increase of 2 per cent in the rate of interest, might be imposed upon them by reason of a visitation of Providence.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This matter was discussed at a provincial conference. I believe I must pead guilty to being the Al-
Dominion Lands Act

berta representative. Mr. Martin represented Saskatchewan, and, I believe, Mr. Norris represented Manitoba. Inasmuch as the interest received from the sale of school lands played such an important part in the revenues for the running of our public schools, we were anxious that large amounts outstanding should be collected. It was suggested at that conference that this was one way to hasten that collection, and we all agreed to it. I must take my share of the responsibility. The object that we had in view was to get in those large outstanding amounts of interest that had accrued against those lands and to utilize them, of course, for the carrying on of our educational work in the provinces. Therefore, in fairness to the federal government, I think they should be given only their share of the responsibility. That was our hope. Unfortunately, in subsequent years, we have had drouth in most of the western provinces, and this is somewhat of a hardship on people owning school lands. I think, however, my hon. friend will agree with me that we did this with the best intention in the world, in the hope that we would assist struggling school districts who needed so badly the distribution of the school funds in all the provinces.

Section agreed to.
On section 7, paragraph (b)-Limits of areas of timber limits.

There is possibly an error in paragraph (b), or, perhaps, I do not read it correctly. The paragraph reads:
Permits to cut timber as cordwood, pulpwood, fence posts or telegraph poles for mining purposes.
Should not that be "telegraph poles or props for mining purposes?" There are no telegraph poles for mining purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had not noticed that before; the hon. member is right.

While the minister is making the correction I would ask him this question. Does this amendment relate to the order in council which was passed early in the year? I cannot recall the exact terms of it, but I read it some months ago and 1 remember that it provides for certain things with reference to pulpwood areas in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, this is a different matter. Our difficulty, I may explain, lies in the areas where we want to give permits to individuals to take out pulpwood, cordwood and so forth. Take British Columbia, for instance. In a large part of that province these areas are under the forestry

regulations and can be let under lease only so that the small man has no opportunity to get in at all. We' cannot at present give him any permit to cut his fence posts or take out cord wood, and this gives the small man the opportunity he has not heretofore enjoyed.
Is it not a pretty wide and general power that is taken here? It is all to be done by the Governor in Council, iipparently without any restrictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are subject to restrictions, with the exception that in the burnt areas the dues are one-half those that obtain in the green timber areas; and when the cut wood is measured the full dues are charged on all that is not burnt.
That is provided for elsewhere, I suppose.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I move to amend paragraph (b) by inserting after the word "poles" in line 38 the words "or props for mining purposes."

On section 5, subsection 1-Issue of shares without nominal or par value.
This clause is either new or it is a departure from the old act. Will the minister give an explanation of it?

The amending act of 1917 provided for the issue of shares without nominal or par value. This is a method of company organization which has prevailed for many years on the continent of Europe. After a prolonged consideration and discussion, the first legislation authorizing shares without par value was introduced in the state of New York in the year 1912. It was from this statute that the amending act of 1917 was adopted. Even at that time the legislation was, to some extent, experimental. It was doubtful whether complications would arise in the organization of companies under these provisions and whether they would meet with the approval of financial interests. In the United States the legislation has been very successful, and the number of companies having shares without par value is steadily increasing. Many of them are quoted on the exchanges, and it is quite apparent that this method meets business interests.

Companies Act
Since 1917 this legislation has developed in the United States. Moreover it has been found that this development has been due to business requirements. The principal change aas been brought about to meet the following circumstances.
As the act stood in the amendment of 1917, a company could not commence business until the total amount of its preferred shares of $5 on each share without par value had been subscribed and paid up. In cases of reorganization this created no difficulty, but it largely prevented new enterprises being undertaken under this method. The regulations of the Department of the Interior require that all oil companies holding leases in the Northwest Territories must be incorporated under this provision. For such companies this section created almost impossible difficulties.
Under the section as amended, section 26 of the act is applicable under paragraph (b) of subsection 4, and the company may commence business as soon as 10 per cent of its capital is subscribed. This would, undoubtedly, mean 10 per cent of the preferred shares and one tenth of the number of shares without nominal or par value.
Moreover, under the amending act of 1917 there was some doubt whether preferred shares without par value could be issued. Many of the companies' acts of the different states provide for preferred shares without par value where the preference is only to the extent of dividend. The section, as amended by the bill, also permits the issue of such shares. Subsection 7b was taken, with verbal alterations, from the legislation of the state of New York for the year 1912. This has been the law of several of the states in the United States since 1912. This section is intended to give us a little more definite information as to the working of the act.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure with respect to freight rates for the carriage of grain by lake and river navigation, and to provide,-
1.	That an3r shipping company or any shipowner or person who carries or who offers, advertises or proposes to carry grain for hire between Fort William or Port Arthur and any other port or place in Canada or the United States of America, by lake or river navigation, shall within a prescribed period file with the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada the tariff of rates which is proposed to be charged, and also any change or variation of such tariff of rates.
2.	That the said board shall receive and tabulate all such tariffs and rates, and ascertain by all available means the rates of freight which prevail or are exacted for the carriage of grain as aforesaid, and report to the minister the facts in respect to deficiency of cargo space, excessive freight charge, or discrimination in rates, and all shippers shall upon request furnish the board with such information as they possess relating to these matters.
3.	That when in the opinion of the board the rates are unreasonable and excessive, the board may prescribe such maximum rates as it may consider reasonable, which may be varied or limited in their operation as the board may prescribe.
4.	That provisions be made as to the posting in the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and in the office of the Board of Grain Commissioners by vessel brokers and agents of statements in detail of cargo space, time for shipment and destination on contracts or charters made on the day last preceding, and to prohibit any vessel broker or agent from soliciting any risk, or issuing or delivering any receipt-or policy of insurance, or collecting or receiving any premium in whole or in part, or inspecting any risk or adjusting any loss upon any consignment of grain to be carried.
5.	That penalties be enacted for the violation of the provisions of the proposed legislation.
Motion agreed to and House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

This is a very important resolution, dealing with a matter of more than passing concern both to the country and to the various interests affected I do not rise at all for the purpose of unfairly or unkindly criticizing the resolution, but I am anxious to have as much information as possible on a number of questions. I trust therefore that the minister will not feel that I am in any way trying to embarrass him. If the questions I ask do not seem particularly relevant to the first subsection under consideration I would ask that they be allowed notwithstanding that fact, because the whole discussion

might very well centre to a large extent around the first section. First of all, I should like to know what reason there is for submitting to the Grain Commission rather than to the Railway Board the question as to the fixation of lake rates. The Grain Commission have no machinery, nor have they experts as in an established department; whereas the Railway Board, having the advantage of many years' experience, and equipped with the necessary technical and clerical machinery, are well organized and able to study any question of this kind. First of all the minister might outline the reasons why this important matter should be placed under the jurisdiction of the Grain Commissioners rather than before the Railway Board.

The Grain Commission have charge of the handling of grain, and are in touch with the elevators at the head of the lakes and the interior elevators. Furthermore, they have a perfect knowledge of the grain, first back in the country and next at the terminal elevators at the head of the lakes and in the elevators east of them. The bill to be introduced based upon this resolution provides not only for the fixing of the maximum rate, but for the regulation of the method of shipping and for the advising of the public as to space available. Early last summer, I think in the month of July, the government had complaints from certain shippers, some of them large shippers, that there was discrimination in the freight rates on the upper lakes as between Canadian and United States ports. There was a difference of opinion between the shippers and the lake carriers. The government tried to induce the lake carriers to remove this discrimination, which they themselves admitted. The carriers, however, contended that the rates quoted to Buffalo were what are known as "distress" rates; on account of strikes in the United States in the coal areas many vessels that otherwise would be carrying coal and iron were offering to carry freight from Fort William and Port Arthur to Buffalo at very much lower rates than the rates charged generally by Canadian companies. We urged upon the Canadian companies that if they could afford to carry grain to Buffalo at rates they themselves admitted, they should at least carry it to Port Colbome at a very small percentage over those rates. The experience of past years was that, generally speaking, they got a quarter of a cent a bushel more to Port Colborne than to Buffalo; in some cases the rate charged was considerably more-almost double. Unfortunately we were unable to induce them to deal fairly

Lake Grain Rates
with Canadian shippers, there being no machinery that we could invoke for the purpose.
Now, based upon this resolution a bill will be introduced providing that shipowners and ship brokers shall file with the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada the rates at which they charter vessels*. It will be the duty of the board to secure such information and have it on file for the minister. Certain penalties will be imposed upon shipowners who refuse to file their rates. I may say that they now give this information to our statistical department, but it comes to us too late to be of any use. If in the judgment of the board the rates charged out of Fort William or Port Arthur are excessive as compared with the rates charged for similar traffic from United States ports, it will be within its power to fix a maximum rate. Of course, this power must be exercised with discretion. A maximum rate must be a fair rate based upon the traffic available for the ships that are doing business. If this maximum rate is fixed too high, the shipowner may consider it the minimum rate; on the other hand, if it is fixed too low it may drive shipping away altogether from Canadian ports over to Duluth, and it might divert our grain to that port, or the shipowner might tie up his vessels. I admit at once that in my judgment we cannot compel any shipowner to run his boats if he is not satisfied with the maximum rate we fix. Therefore, as I say. care and discretion must, and we expect will, be exercised in this regard. We believe that the Board of Grain Commissioners at the head of the lakes, being conversant with the conditions of the grain trade from day to day, are in a much better position to handle this rate question intelligently than a board located at Ottawa far away from the scene of operations. This is one reason which induced the government to select the Board of Grain Commissioners for this purpose.
Right here I may say that in addition to these powers the bill will provide for the preventing of what is regarded by the producers and shippers of grain as an unfair method of booking space; that is, of the vessel broker or agent saying to the shipper: "Unless you take insurance with me you cannot have the space you require." We propose to get rid of this trouble by prohibiting the broker or agent from either writing the insurance or inspecting any risk.
This, generally speaking is an outline of the bill. The government invites advice from the House. We do not believe that this proposal will be a cure-all, but it is an honest effort, through publicity primarily, to
obtain reasonable rates for the shippers of grain.

Are there any
penalties besides publicity?

Yes, quite severe penalties.
We do not want to go through the experience of last season. Early in the season it was aomplained that there was discrimination as between Canadian and United States ports: later on the complaint was that the rates were unduly advanced. As regards the latter complaint, I am bound to say that from the information I have gathered the blame was not all on one side. I understand the exporters sold for export large quantities of grain without taking the precaution of securing lake space. They bought their ocean space and intended to route the grain by Buffalo to American ports. As soon as the coal strike was settled and cars were requisitioned to carry coal, Buffalo fell down and instead of putting out a thousand cars a day the number fell to about two hundred, and, of course, Buffalo became congested. Thereupon the grain was brought around to Montreal and Quebec and the exporters put their brokers in the pit and offered the shipowners advanced rates. As a result a good many of the exporters lost money, particularly the United States exporters. Now, while the exporters lost money on the grain exported early in the year, the loss backed up on the crop in the country and depressed the price of the grain which later came on the market. We are attempting to regulate this traffic so there will be more reasonable rates for the carriage of grain, and so that the shippers will have every day during the shipping season at Fort William, Port Arthur and Winnipeg information as to what space has been booked and what is still available. We hope through publicity-which after all is the great curative agency-that the rates prevailing during the coming season will be fairer than they were last season.

have power last year to suspend the coasting laws?
Mr, ROBB:	That power was exercised
by our predecessors under the War Measures Act, and we exercised it last year, to cover grain carried across the lakes for storage so that we might have the business for our own railways. But if the matter had been taken to the courts I am not sure whether our action could have been upheld.

If there is discrimination against Canadian ports in relation to the rates obtaining to American ports, is not that

the obvious and quickest method of overcoming it? Under this legislation you cannot empower the Grain Commission to
10 p.m. fix a rate from Fort William to Buffalo, or from Duluth to Port Colborne. To put it another way, it will be impossible for parliament to confer power on the Grain Commission to fix rates from a Canadian port to an American port or vice versa. Now if we recognize that, then there is but very little force in the law to fix it from one Canadian port to another, because the diversion from the Canadian port to the American port will then follow as a natural sequence to the limit of the capacity of the American receiving ports. I think that is obvious. The only remedy would be to suspend the coasting laws. Then you effectively cover'the discrimination or the excess rate. What I am trying to impress upon the minister, and what I really think the committee should consider, is whether it is advisable at all to frame a law which may give the impression that you are going to deal with a problem but which in its essence will not deal with the problem at all. That is, I think, the point we ought to consider in this committee, and it is a very important consideration.	*
I do not want to embarrass the minister with too many questions, but he is well acquainted with this matter and will follow me, and then I shall not have to bother him so much later on. Take the question of demurrage. If the Board of Grain Commissioners is to have power to fix rates they certainly twill have to take into consideration the question of demurrage. Now I submit this, that no shipping company can possibly gauge or anticipate what would be an exactly fair rate unless it knows what the demurrage is going to be. If they take a chance on demurrage and the demurrage seems to be threatening seriously, the rates are going to go up. There ifi no question about that. It is the only protection the shipping company has. So if a shipping company anticipating a demurrage increases its rate for its own protection, w'hich it would have a right to do, the Grain Board might step in and say: Your rates are too high, atid it would reduce the rates and the shipping company would lose unfairly because of demurrage over which it has no control at all. These, I think, are very important considerations.
While I have the most profound sympathy with the desire to lower the cost of transportation I am very, very doubtful if you are going to do it by this bill at all. In fact, I really think that the net result of this bill

will be to maintain generally speaking a higher rate. As it is to-day there have been and very frequently are periods when rates are abnormally low. Then occasionally like last year there comes a period when the rate is abnormally and perhaps unfairly high, but these periods of excessively high rates are comparatively rare, so that in the main I think in the past the lower rates have fairly well compensated for the higher. But if you give power to a commission such as the Grain Board to fix rates I am firmly convinced of this from my study of the question, and this same problem was threshed out in the House on several occasions in years gone by, that the average cost for transporting grain over the Great Lakes year in and year out will be higher than if there were no fixation of rates. What I do think is this, that the minister or the government could adequately and safely provide against these abnormal, excessive rates in occasional periods by a vigorous yet careful application of the suspension of the coasting laws. Let it be clearly understood and known that that may happen; let that weapon be ready at hand and be looked upon as a remedy.
The minister perhaps has already given consideration to all these points. I would like to ask him to give to the committee the fullest possible information and answer to these suggestions because to me they are very important. I am very, very much afraid that the net result of this legislation in its working out will be to make the average rate year in and year out higher than it has been in the past.

May I point out in reply to what my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has said that at the present time the American government are exercising a similar power of fixing a maximum rate. It does not apply to bulk freight, I believe, but to other freight.
There is also this point: During the last shipping season the rates between Canadian ports were higher than the rates from Canadian ports to American ports. Also the rates charged .by Canadian boats from one Canadian point to another Canadian point were higher than those charged between American points. While some are under the impression that this power ought to be placed in the hands of the Railway Commission it seems to me that it would work much better if it were placed in the hands of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and for this reason: The Board of Grain Commissioners are more closely in touch with the producers, and the producers are practically the only losers when rates go astray as they did last session. Let me follow that up. The price of the grain that we sell, even though it may be sold right at the elevator, is based on the price of the same grain at Liverpool or London less all the costs of transportation, insurance, and so forth. If you will read carefully the report of the Grain Commission which has just been handed in you will find this statement:	That so far as insurance is
concerned the shippers do not care very much what insurance they pay so long as they can get as good a rate as their competitors. In a report that was handed in by the commission that investigated the grain trade in, I think, 1914-1 refer to the commission appointed by the Saskatchewan government- you will also find this statement.
That the shippers care very little what lake rates they pay provided they can get as good rates as their competitors.
Now, that is the point. Some people suppose that the shippers are very anxious to fight for low rates, but that is not the case. They care very little what the rates are so long as their competitors get no better rates than they enjoy. The Board of Grain Commissioners at the present time is composed of three men. Two of the number grew up
with farming in the West, grew up with the various organizations that were established there, and I think members of this House will recognize that those who have once lived on the farm and know the difficulties that have to be overcome are likely to have a greater sympathy and understanding of. the problem, and the obstacles that need to be surmounted, than those who have not had that experience. The minister has just said he will not admit that is the case. I suppose he means that the shippers sometimes sustained losses last year. mission might as well have been in Jerusalem; I think the western public had practically no confidence in it. That is a strong statement to make but if hon. members had suffered as long as the western farmer has suffered by reason of neglect they perhaps would be ready to make statements just as strong. The change now accomplished has been very much for the better. I have heard the present chairman of the board spoken of very highly. I know the other two gentlemen and I have the greatest confidence in their integrity and ability. I therefore am inclined to look with favour on the placing of this matter under the Board of Grain Commissioners.

I should like to ask
the minister what legal position he thinks the government were in last year with regard to the suspension of the coasting law? I understood him to say that the suspension under the former government was made under the War Measures Act. But there was a suspension of the coasting laws in 1913, and I understand that this government could have exercised last fall the same power that was exercised by the former government in 1913.
The suspension of the coasting laws is not dealt with in this resolution. It will come up later in a resolution to be brought forward by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

I wish to make a few remarks at this particular time but not at any great length; we will have an opportunity of further discussion when the bill to be founded on this resolution is taken up in committee. At the risk of being tedious I must say a few words by way of introduction about the condition of the western farmer and the interest he feels in the provision of this resolution. I know that sometimes the producers of the West are very much sympathized with in this House. I should like to say, however, that, perhaps, the epic of the western prairie provinces has never yet been written. The story of the struggles, the courage, the patience, and the industry of those determined and courageous people who developed the prairies has never yet been adequately recognized. I know very well the problem to be solved is looked upon with a great deal of sympathy but sometimes, unfortunately, misstatements and misinformation distort peoples' vision so that they do not get a proper perspective.
As has already been stated, the great problem we have to deal with in the central prairie 
provinces is that of transportation. The agricultural potentialities of that part of Canada are great indeed but unfortunately those rich alluvial soils are located in the very centre of the Dominion and for all time to come transportation will be one of the greatest problems we shall have to solve in developing that country and furthering the prosperity of the people who live there. Last year we waged a strong fight in connection with freight rates and hon. members will not think that I am boasting if I say that we went home thoroughly satisfied with the struggle we had maintained and the conclusion come to in regard to railway rates from the West. But after producing a large crop, after having secured reduction of railway rates, what was the consternation of the people in the West when they learned that all the advantage that had been gained in that freight rate reduction was to be absorbed by an increase in lake freights. [DOT]
I have listened to the remarks made by the minister (Mr. Robb) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). Those remarks were very fair I admit and each gentleman perhaps, presented the case from his own standpoint. But we are always met with the same stoi-y when we attempt to remedy an abuse-we must be very careful for fear we shall hamper business in any way. Now, I realize the situation just as well as any hon. member of this House but I must confess I think the members of the lake shipping combine, if you will let me use the term, are quite capable of taking care of themselves. They will be able to do so no matter what kind of legislation you pass here. I have heard the same story before, it is not new to me. "That if you hamper trade we will move over to the United States and leave you in the lurch altogether." I do not think there is' any danger of that. These people will stay just as long as there is any business for them to do, and they will get their share of that business and get their profits-there is no doubt about it.
Now, what happened? I am not going to-review the whole situation because there will be other opportunities of doing that, but we know that at the beginning of the season the rates had been fixed at three cents per bushel from Bay ports to Buffalo. Then came this enormous crop, and we had that famous meeting that took place in Toronto in May 1922,. when half a dozen shipping companies got together and formed what you may call a 'combine, because there is no other name that would be appropriate for it, and they agreed

Lake Grain Rates
to fix the rate at 7 or 8 cents immediately after. I do not think there was any congestion at Buffalo at the time these rates were increased to that amount. The rates went even higher than that. I will mention another fact in connection with the brokerage and shipping agents. As has been stated already, the brokers had claimed the right of getting the insurance when they gave space, and I think we find it in the evidence in this report,-at least the evidence was submitted, or published in the papers, during the time that commission was taking evidence-that when a shipper would go to a broker in the city of Winnipeg and ask for space, even although he knew the rate had been fixed at 3 cents, he was frequently told the rate was 7 cents, and when the question of insurance was brought up he made the remark that he was able to insure himself, and he was told, "If you do not place the insurance with me you cannot have space." We know that in the season of 1922 the brokerage agents got about $448,000 of commissions for selling insurance. As high as $2,000 commission was paid on insuring some cargoes of grain.

Did the Winnipeg brokers
charge a greater premium for this insurance than it could be got for outside?

Just 100 per cent more than the rate which could have been obtained from private operators or companies furnishing insurance themselves. It was double in many cases. There is another peculiar situation in regard to this matter. When the question of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine came up-and I think the hon. member for Lunenburg will be wide awake now-
I am awake all right.

When the Canadian Government Merchant Marine came up for discussion, we were told the government had no vessels fit to carry grain. I find in the evidence submitted before the commission that at the very time the trouble was taking place on the lakes the government had 10 or 11 boats fit for carrying grain, and they had 'leased two grain carrying boats to one of the shipping companies in that combine. I do not know why these vessels were tied up, or not in commission, and why they were not carrying grain or doing something to break up that combination on the lakes at that particular time. Perhaps the minister will be able to give us some information on that point. I think perhaps there is an idea sometimes of driving the trade to Buffalo instead of to the Bay ports or other Canadian ports.
We hear a great deal about mixing grain, and it pays the shipper sometimes to mix grain, and perhaps it is a disadvantage that our grain should be shipped by Buffalo any more than we can possibly help. I believe in letting the grain go to the ocean by the cheapest route no matter where that route is. That is the only method and system that will stand the test of time. We were told that those government vessels were unfit for carrying grain. I was rather chagrined the other day, on reading the report of the Senate proceedings, to notice that Senator Bennett had made some nice statements about my sincerity and honesty, but he was rather sorry for my ignorance in regard to this matter, because I had innocently asked if there were no Canadian boats able to carry grain. He immediately stated that there were five or six Canadian ships suited for carrying grain on the Great Lakes. I do not know the facts, but these are the statements made, and I have no doubt the speaker had some reason for making them.
I think there were six government boats in commission last fall on the upper lakes.
The phrase used was that they were "tied up" on the lakes.

The hon. member is quite right. They were tied up until the government came in and insisted-notwithstanding the statement that we should not interfere in their management of these roads-that these ships should be put into commission, and that was done.
At what rate?
The government has nothing to do with the operation of the roads. The government keeps its hands off that. That is done by the management of the railway.

I have an idea that this Canadian Government Merchant Marine entered the combine and charged the same rates as the other boats were charging. I know there is that old school of politicians known as the Manchester School, that never believed in interference in trade but wished to remove all restrictions and allow each individual to operate for himself; claiming that everything would come right by competition. But a great deal of water has passed under the bridge since that time, and a great many things taken place that those economists knew nothing about. Combinations in restraint of trade and gigantic combines were not known in those days, and, if hon. members
Lake Grain Bates

will allow a vulgar phrase, sometimes you have to fight the devil with his own weapons, and when we take into consideration combinations and restrictions to prevent the free interchange of trade, it becomes absolutely necessary that there should be some law guiding and controlling freights and other methods of doing business with these combinations.
I would like to say a few words in regard to who pays the bill. I know that it gets tiresome in this House to be continually falling back on the farmer, but really, Mr. Chairman, I have forgotten all my economics if I cannot see that the cost always falls back on the producer-I do not care what line of business it is. I have had a good deal to do with business in the way of paying taxes, and I find among the men and merchants doing business on the prairies there is a great deal of grumbling about taxation. How is taxation levied? Simply on the cost of doing business, and it has to come back to the production of the soil, and the man on the farm is paying the taxes. The man on the farm in western Canada pays the bill, I do not care what restrictions you put on.
It may happen that in the raising of freight rates, or in some other way, the shipper loses money on one ship load, but, take it on the whole, the cost of doing business and the increased cost of transportation must fall back on the producer.
Last year we heard a great deal about the enormous crop produced in western Canada. We heard about 400,000,000 bushels of wheat being produced there. We were told about the great stream of wealth that flowed from the western prairie down to eastern Canada and helped to revive trade and set things moving all over the country. Is it not a tragedy, and is it not something to be sorry for when we realize that the people who raised that great amount of wealth have not reaped the benefit, and are worse off to-day than perhaps a year ago? Is it not strange that there should be perhaps a little work-up over any combination that will put a charge on every bushel of wheat the farmers produce? Already we are beginning to hear that next year we are going to produce 500,000,000 bushels of wheat; and what is happening? We find the price is dropping rapidly, on the theory that there is going to be a large production next season. No one can tell what the crops will be on the prairie. Those who know anything about western conditions will know that in two weeks' time the crops will either be made or broken, according to climatic conditions. The prospects are good to-day, but, no one can tell what they will be in the month of August.

I will not take up any more time at the present. We have the recommendations made by the commission which sat and took evidence in this matter. For my part, I would be inclined to accept those recommendations as they have been made by the commission. I have no fear that they will not work out to the benefit and advantage of everyone concerned. I have no fear of any commission ever fixing maximum rates at a figure that will damage lake shipping to any great extent. Producers even are reasonable, and I think they will be willing to pay a fair rate for getting their grain shipped across the Great Lakes. I shall have an opportunity of speaking to this question again. I have made only a few remarks, and I hope the committee will give the matter very serious consideration, because it affects, not only western Canada, but the prosperity of the Dominion.

I cannot profess that I know very much concerning the facts at issue in this particular matter which is before the committee, but I am somewhat perplexed as to what should be my duty upon this measure. I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Forke) has minimized my difficulties in the matter, because he has hardly made reference to the legislation which is before the committee; that is, he fails to demonstrate whether or not it would be effective and, in the ultimate end, a measure in the interest of the people of Canada and in the interest of the particular class in which he is concerned
I failed to say that, perhaps, the publicity which will be given to the whole affair will be the best cure for the conditions complained of.

I do not mean to suggest that my hon. friend has yet exhausted all his arguments. I merely mean to say that, up to the point reached in his remarks, he did not touch upon those features of this proposed legislation which, to me at least, are objectionable, unless I have some explanation to the contrary. For those whose products must find their outlet to the ocean, in this particular case through the Great Lakes, I have every sympathy, and I presume every hon. gentleman in this House has. The question, however, is: Will this legislation bring about any desired end? Is it wise legislation? Ultimately, will it be in the interest of the producer, the shipper or the country generally?

It is better than no legislation at all.

I doubt that very much. Ineffective legislation is frequently worse than no legislation, and I may refer to that before I take my seat. As I said before, I hardly know the facts that were revealed before the commission, but I understand that the charge is that unconscionably high rates were exacted by owners of shipping on the Great Lakes. If that is true, it was wrong, and the question before the committee is: How are we going to remedy that wrong? We ought to approach the question in that spirit, and it should not be said by hon. gentlemen who are, perhaps, particularly interested because many of their constituents are shippers, that because one is disposed to doubt the efficacy of the legislation, therefore, he is opposed to the interest of those people. I resent that form of argument, and it should not be tolerated in legislative halls. I hope it will not be too frequently made.
I do not think I was guilty of that.

No, but somebody else said that. The newspapers have discussed this matter; but again I say that my reading would be quite casual, and I would not like to predicate an argument upon it. I suppose a great deal of evidence was taken, and I presume it will be printed before we proceed much further with the bill. A few days ago we were discussing the Bank Act, and the evidence was printed daily. The Bank Act was a fairly simple subject. It might be discussed in a young ladies' seminary or a kindergarten school with great ease and be made plain to everybody. I do not mean to *say that banking itself or finance generally is an easy subject; but when you are dealing with a concrete question such as the Bank Act, it is quite easy.

Has the hon. member seen to-night's paper with the report of the Union Bank in it?
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax); Yes. I do not know what my hon. friend wants to draw from that.
Is it a very simple matter?

I do not think It is anything that will reflect upon the actions of the majority of the committee. It -might cause some misgivings on the part of some other hon. gentlemen, including, perhaps, my hon. friend. The point I want to make is this: Last night I heard for, I suppose, the hundredth time, that it was unfair and unjust to proceed to the consideration of .a measure Which had been before a committee for two months, until the people had had an opportunity of reading and studying the evidence. The evidence in that case had been printed daily, and it was before the country and parliament. I want to suggest to the minister that he is going to meet with tremendous opposition from our hon. friends directly opposite, because I am sure they will not consent to a favourable consideration of the bill until the evidence is printed, so that they may know what they are doing.
How long is it since the report of the commission was tabled?
That is the report of a commission, a report made by three men who are not infallible.
Were the members of the Banking committee infallible?

I did not allege that at all. I merely mean to say-and I am sure everybody opposite to me will agree and they must say that later this evening- that it would be unfair and unjust to proceed further in this matter until the evidence is printed, so that we may know what we are doing and whatever course we shall take
They will have stolen another crop if we wait that length of time.
I might suggest that we put them in gaol first, and then wait for the evidence.
Is the hon. member aware that the fact of a combination between the shipping companies was proved and is within the knowledge of the House now?
I do not quite jnderstand my hon. friend's question.
Perhaps the hon. member does not wish to answer.
I thought it was a good opportunity to remind my hon. friends right opposite me that this might be a good chance to be consistent upon such an important question.
Do I understand that my hon. friend now adopts the arguments that were propounded from this side of the House yesterday?

No. I do not go even so far as to say that I would personally demand the printing of the evidence. I am simply advising the minister that he must expect most powerful opposition from hon. gentlemen opposite to this bill being pro-
Lake Grain Rates

ceeded with further until the evidence is printed, so that they may know what they are doing.
The hon. member for Halifax thinks misery likes company. He would like to see the minister in the same box.

The subject involved in this resolution has been before this House on many occasions in the past. 1 was always opposed to it and I think the majority of members of parliament were usually opposed to it. I shall still be opposed to the principle involved in this resolution, unless I hear some stronger reasons to the contrary from some hon. gentlemen who may yet speak. I refer to the motions that were made annually by Mr. Armstrong, one of the members from Ontario, motions which practically covered the same ground as this resolution purports to cover. In so far as the bill proposes taking powers to suspend the coasting laws, I do not object to it. Perhaps that is a fair power for the Governor in Council to have for many reasons, and in view of rhe report of the commission, I do not complain that that power is proposed to be taken by the minister. If there was a combine, and if there was exacted excessively high, unconscionable rates, it is our duty, by amending the general law, the Combines Act, to meet that case. That surely is a fair proposition; and if it is possible to meet that particular situation, then I say it should be met by an amendment to the general law. I object to paternal legislation and to all efforts to meet by means of specific enactments every little grievance.
I should not like my hon. friend to go the length of adopting the laissez faire policy of the Manchester School of economists. I remember that when I first learned that Bright and Cobden had opposed some labour legislation which seemed obviously defensible I was astounded. I do admit that, as we progress, special legislation must be introduced to meet special conditions of the day; but I do not think that this is a case in which we should adopt the legislation proposed in the resolution. The resolution proposes to control prices. Now freight is a commodity like anything else, and I do not know of any case where prices have been successfully controlled. It is possible that during the war many countries successfully exercised some control over prices in different directions.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that there is some comparison between this question and the Railway Commission?

No; I shall come to that later. I was observing that during the war, when imports and exports were controlled, a control of prices was possible and perhaps successful, although since then economists who have studied the question have declared that price control was unsuccessful and disastrous. I was reading only yesterday a book by an eminent European economist who, discussing this very matter, contends that during the war high prices were due not to the exactions of middlemen, or of trusts, or of any combinations of that character, but to great inflation of credit, which produced competition for the world's output. I think the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) and one of the hon. members for Calgary would agree with that view; the rise of prices was due to that cause rather than to any great profits exacted by producers and sellers. I admit, of course, that in many cases there was profiteering of a very objectionable nature.

If the hon. member has read the report carefully he will find that the commissioners state that the rates on all commodities on the lakes except grain are controlled in one way or another. By a contractual arrangement the rates on ore, which is one of the largest cargoes carried, and on coal as well, are controlled. The commissioners declare that everything is controlled except grain.

I am not contending that there was not a combination and that, perhaps, some remedial legislation is not necessary. I am simply arguing that the proposal contained in the resolution does not provide the proper procedure. Some hon. gentlemen asked me a few moments ago whether, if it was fair to' control railway rates, it was not equally fair to control shipping rates. I say there is no analogy whatever between the two cases. The railways constitute a monopoly in this country, as in all countries. The construction of railways must of necessity be limited, so that in all respects railways are a monopoly that should be controlled. No person or corporation is permitted to build railways in this country in competition with existing lines without statutory authority because it is not deemed prudent to allow people to build such railways everywhere they please; it is not considered in the national interests. On the contrary, it is considered wise from the national point of view to select the corporations who shall be allowed to build and operate railways. So that with deliberation the state constitutes a monopoly in this regard. In shipping, the analogous case would consist in confining steamship operations

Lake Grain Rates
on the Great Lakes to one or two or three lines and then controlling rates. That would be analogous to the railway situation, and the control of rates in that case might be justifiable. Still no one would support that view. Again I doubt whether this parliament has the jurisdiction to enact the legislation proposed in the resolution. I do not believe there is one single proposal in the resolution that ultimately will be held to be within the legislative powers of this parliament. More than that, I doubt very much the wisdom-
Would the hon. gentleman specify his reasons for doubting parliament's jurisdiction?

As I say, I doubt very much the wisdom, if there is any doubt about the jurisdiction, of enacting this legislation. We do not want to go through the same experience we had in connection with the Board of Commerce. I am not going to give my reasons for my doubts as to the competency of this parliament to pass this legislation. The opinion of the law officers of the Crown should be made known to parliament and whatever it is it will be acceptable to me.
The Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) approved of it
I really do not know that he has.
Well, he has through his government.
For that matter legislation is frequently presented to parliament by governments without any special attention having been given to the question of jurisdiction or constitutionality
Then he is not competent to be Minister of Justice.

Whenever the question is raised I think it will be the duty of the Department of Justice to give it consideration and advise parliament in the premises. Now, if it is fair to introduce this legislation in respect of shipping on the Great Lakes, someone will come along and say that the same thing should be done on the Pacific coast or on the Atlantic. We have free trade m shipping.
No, we have not.
Well, subject to the alleged combination; it is qualified of course, to that extent. But there is nothing to prohibit anybody going into the lake freight business.
When you recollect that there are six strong companies doing business on the lakes, is it possible for a single competitor to do business against that combination?

Such competition might ' be difficult. But what would happen if this legislation had the effect of decreasing that number? I do not say that this will happen, but I simply put the question to my hon. friend. I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite, who stand as exponents of legislation which permits an equal opportunity to all; and if those hon. gentlemen take the same point of view as they take in connection with analogous matters, then I am sure they will be opposed to this legislation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in the first place, I doubt the power of parliament to legislate. In the second place, if this measure is put on the statute book I say it will be ineffective. It is an attempt to control prices, and this is always ineffectual. It is unsound, and I do not believe that hon. gentlemen who have spoken in support of the resolution believe in the control of prices. It never gets you anywhere; it hurts everybody and accomplishes no good results.
Does the hon. member believe in this scale of rates last season running from three to eleven cents?

I am not discussing rates at all. Let me repeat, if the rates charged were so excessive as to become what we might term unconscionable, and we think that something should be done to prevent a recurrence', let us amend the AntiCombines Act or pass general legislation which will be applicable to the whole country.

Will the minister tell us if the government have consulted the law officers of the Crown with regard to their power under the Criminal Code to prosecute the men who constituted this combine? I understood that during the investigation two or three of these-I hesitate to call them what their conduct merits; I certainly would not call them Canadians-were down at Palm Beach. But it is altogether likely that they have since returned to Canada. Numerous representations have been made to me on the subject and I am convinced that western Canada in its present mood is going to demand the prosecution of these men. Before I leave the Chamber to-night I should like to know if the government have consulted the law officers of the Crown with regard to their

power to proceed under the Criminal Code. If not, what justification has the minister to give to the House?

Mr. Chairman, I imagine my hon. friend has in mind a prosecution under the Criminal Code. I am not a legal man, but I would advise my hon. friend that if any one in western Canada desires to prosecute the persons referred to, the Criminal Code is open to him as to anyone else. In reply to my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) I gather he is in favour of the legislation proposed in the next resolution for the suspension of the coasting laws, but that he objects to the government gathering the very information necessary before we can intelligently decide whether or not we should suspend those laws.

I do not object to the proposal to suspend the coasting laws, because there seems to be a general demand for such suspension and many people think it might prevent a repetition of what occurred last year. I do not believe in it as a matter of principle, but I conceive it may be necessary at the present time.

But the government before deciding whether suspension is necessary or not must have certain information. This bill will empower the Board of Grain Commissioners to gather such information from time to time. This should satisfy my hon. friend that part of the legislation at least is necessary. My hon. friend doubts the legality of this proposed legislation. I am bound to admit that it may be challenged before the courts and declared illegal. The Grain Act was taken into the courts, but the gentlemen who did so are sorry to-day because they have cast some doubt upon that legislation. It is always possible to destroy the usefulness of measures which are enacted for the good of the people generally, for there are always clever lawyers ready to plead their clients' case. I am not prepared to say whether some one might not successfully contest the validity of this bill after its enactment, but it has been prepared by the law officers of the Crown, and the government believe in its legality.
Would the minister state upon what advice the Governor in Council would be prepared to act in suspending the coasting laws?

That would be determined
later after the necessary information was secured. Last year the government received telephone messages urging the suspension of

the coasting laws. We replied that we must have something in writing, and eventually we received telegrams. But other gentlemen telegraphed the government that it was not necessary to suspend the coasting laws. This shows the necessity of some machinery for gathering the information we require before we can act intelligently, and what better machinery can we have for this purpose than the Board of Grain Commissioners who understand the necessities of the grain trade?
That is all right.
I have followed with interest the ingenious arguments of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean)-
They were not ingenious at all.

-in his attempt to convince us that we should vote against this bill. As usual, he tendered us his sympathy. We have had a good deal of sympathy already and will have a lot of it to take back to oui people in the West. Of course, it is a very cheap commodity. But I can assure him that he will not find any objection to this bill from this quarter of the House unless I am very much mistaken. His whole argument i* against the fixing of the lake rates. I would reply, Mr. Chairman, that it all depends on who does the fixing. These rates have been fixed a long, long time for us-but not by us. Yesterday the fixing of the bank interest rate was objected to. It has been fixed a good long time. I want to know, Mr. Chairman, why the lake rates should not be controlled. Here we have a magnificent waterway, we have spent millions of dollars on it and we are still spending many more millions. And the people who settled in the West have always hoped that this waterway would be used to convey their grain at very cheap rates. We have been told time and again-by our friends on the right especially, who are so strong in advocating the St. Lawrence route -that the opening of this route will mean a saving of at least five cents a bushel to the farmer on his grain. I have never believed it because experience has shown that the more money we spend on these waterways the higher the rates go. I wonder how the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) would explain this situation-that Canadian boats carry grain from American ports at rates 50 per cent cheaper than from Canadian ports. We find many instances of this discrimination in the evidence taken before the special commission. Here are a few of them. [DOT] Fort William to Port Colborne, 3| cents; Duluth to Port Colborne, 2.1 cents. These

rates were in effect the same day for practically the same distance-perhaps a little farther from Duluth. Fort William to Port McNicoll, 3 cents; Chicago to Depot Harbour, 2 cents. And so on all the way down the line. The finding of the commission is that the rates are practically 50 per cem higher from Canadian ports than
11 p.m. from American. How would my hon. friend justify that? Doe3 he wonder that we think some sort of control is necessary? My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) argued that the producer pays the bill. He certainly does. When the exporter finds it is costing him so much to ship his grain, he makes his bid on the Winnipeg Grain Exchange in accordance with that cost, and the price for the day is communicated to the elevators in the country, thus affecting the farmers' price.
With regard to the situation last fall 1 know that representations were made to the minister to put into effect the suspension of the coasting laws. They were asking a price for May even during the winter which affected every bushel of wheat marketed in the West during all the winter months. But no action was taken by the government until late last fall when boats were used for winter storage. As to the legality, I would point out that such action was taken years ago by the then existing Conservative government by order in council, and its action was never challenged at all.
I was very greatly disappointed with the answer given by the minister that no action would be taken against thes"e men who had been found guilty of fleecing the western producer of millions of dollars. I was very greatly disappointed with his reply that it is open to anybody in the West to prosecute these men. To my mind that is not a satisfactory situation at all, and if this government has the interests of the producer at heart they should if at all possible take action against these men. There is sufficient evidence I think to prove that a combine in restraint of trade existed not only in regard to rates but also in regard to insurance.
I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend's argument, but may I remind him that the administration of the criminal law is left entirely to the provinces.
Then will the minister explain to the committee how he expects to get action under the new anti-Combines Act?

The provinces will have to
prosecute.
I did not understand it that way. I thought when we passed this legislation it had teeth in it and that this government would be able to take action.
Sold again.

Sold again as my hon. friend
says, I believe is correct.

It was brought out in evidence that the representatives of the government line attended those meetings with Mr. Wolvin, Mr. Enderby of the Canada Steamship Lines, and Mr. Matthews of the Matthews Line. Will that combine be considered to have been formed in New York and therefore be regarded as outside the jurisdiction of this country?
