speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend is confusing the question of the administration of the Criminal Code with the carrying into effect of the provisions of the antiCombines Act. The anti-Combines Act that passed this House would not have any effect as regards a combine formed last summer unless it is in existence now. No act is retroactive unless it is specially declared to be so. My hon. friend is familiar with the provisions of the anti-Combines Act, and so far as its provisions relate to this government they will be carried out, but the administration of the Criminal Code rests with the province where the offence is committed.

I was simply taking my hon. friend's statement that the party who should prosecute would be the Attorney General of the province where the offence was committed, and I went on to say that this combine was formed in New York, and wanted to know whether the Criminal Code could be applied in that case, or would it be considered as being outside the jurisdiction of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend had better ask the hon. member for Calgary West, who I understand supplies the law for that side of the House on legal questions.

Why should I be given an answer like that when the Minister of Justice is sitting in his seat? If the disposition of the government is to pass us by with answers such as was given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the one that is now given by the Acting Minister of National Defence, what is the use of our trying to get information? If the Minister of Justice would care to give the information I should be very pleased to receive it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member will be good enough to put his question I will try and answer it. What is the question please?

The question is this: Three of these shipping men who practically control the whole shipping on the Great Lakes so far as Canada is concerned meet in New York with representatives of our government-owned lines and make a combine to fix rates. Now would action against that combine be considered to be outside the jurisdiction of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would prefer to have a little time to consider the question, but answering offhand I would be inclined

to say that this would not constitute a combine on which prosecution could be instituted in this country.
I do not intend to take up any more time at this stage. Anything I have to say on the insurance and brokerage clauses I will say when they come up.

This question of shipping on the Great Lakes is rather an old one. For twenty years or more the shipping interests of the United States have been endeavouring to gain a foothold in what we might call local Canadian shipping. I have been told that some ten or twelve years ago the government, which at that time owned the elevators at Montreal, offered to certain men who were prepared to put up a certain amount of capital for shipping on the Great Lakes the use of the elevators at Montreal without cost providing that they would ship through these elevators five million bushels of wheat. While we may talk about combines, the fact is that certain men in this country made a proposition that they would put their money into a shipping enterprise which would carry wheat and other commodities from the head of the lakes to Montreal. In those days it was a marvellous thing to think that at any time in the future 5,000,000 bushels of wheat might be shipped to the grain elevators of Montreal. So huge an enterprise did it appear that the gentlemen who had the proposition in hand refused to give any undertaking in the matter. But what do we find to-day? Instead of 5,000,000 bushels of wheat, over 150,000,000 bushels last year went through the elevators of Montreal I believe, that a development of such a character is in the interest of Canadian shipping and of Canadian business. My hon. friend from Saltcoats (Mr. Sales), I think it was, said that we had little sympathy with certain propositions which he had to make. Well, personally, as a general rule I am more or less in sympathy with propositions intended to benefit Canadian industry and the Canadian people; but I do not believe we should consider a proposition which will place Canadian shipping on the Great Lakes in the Lands of American companies, as will be the case if this bill becomes law. May I say that I have been reading American papers for some days past, ever since the announcement of this proposed legislation was made, and it i3 a marvellous thing to consider that within twenty-four hours from the time it became known an American company was formed at Duluth for the purpose of interfering-shall I say?-with Canadian and American trade-

Lake G\ 11 Rates
Competing would be better.

No I say interfering; it is not a case of competing. I will answer my hon. friend by saying this: If our government had made certain propositions whereby our Canadian coasting vessels on the Great Lakes would be given the same rights in the United States as this bill proposes to give American shipping in Canada, I would say it was a fair proposition.
We have got that provision in our law.
I should like to see it.

It is to be found in section 958 of the Shipping Act which provides that:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, declare that the foregoing provisions of this part shall not apply to the ships or vessels of any foreign country in which British ships are admitted to the coasting trade of such country, and to carry goods and passengers from one port or place to another in such country.
So we already have this provision in our law.

Has the minister had any undertaking on behalf of the American government that the thing will be made effective? Certainly not, but we are giving away certain rights that we have on the Great Lakes which I think we should hold dear and sacred. While I do not wish to oppose a government measure I consider the time has come when we as Canadians should uphold our rights and privileges, and treat as they deserve any company or any combine who may propose to take away from us those trading rights which American companies will enjoy if this bill goes into effect.
My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) made some observations as to the constitutionality of this question. Well, I think he is right. However, I am not going into that question at all. I say we have developed a trade on the Great Lakes which we are foolish to abandon to competitors in the United States.

Whom does my hon.
friend mean by "we?"

I mean we Canadians.
Perhaps my hon. friend does not belong to that class; I am afraid he does not. I mean that we Canadians have developed a trade on the Great Lakes which we should preserve [DOT]to the utmost of our ability. My hon. friend asks "Who are we?" Propositions were made years ago, as I have already said, to various 270
shipping interests to gt into this business and attempt to draw the \ rain trade from Fort William and the various lake ports to Montreal. They have done that successfully but I do say this: If they have combined to charge unjustifiable freight rates on the upper lakes they should be brought to task; but it is unfair, and the argument cannot be justified, to maintain that we should throw open our ports to American interests, and permit them to divert our grain trade from Montreal or Quebec to United States ports. I am that kind of an American-
Oh, oh.

Or I should say rather
that kind of Canadian.

Is my hon. friend aware
that the amount of grain going through American ports has increased steadily during the last three or four years, and that at the present time the Canadian boats are giving the preference to Buffalo-that is carrying grain much cheaper to Buffalo than to Canadian ports?
I am not aware of that.
It is a fact all the same.

I am aware of this fact- that twelve years ago we were shipping
5.000.	000 bushels a week to the ports of Montreal and Quebec and to-day we are shipping
150.000.	000 bushels to those same ports.

I rather think you must
be wrong in your dates.

Then let my hon. friend
correct me.
The port of Montreal was under the Harbour Commission more than twelve years ago.

Perhaps I should say
thirteen years ago. I obtained authoritative figures from the Department of Trade and Commerce and Marine and Fisheries.
There is another aspect of this question I would like to discuss very briefly. A commission investigated the freight rates on the Great Lakes, and I have no hesitation in saying that the three gentlemen that composed it were three very excellent men. But I would suggest to you, Sir, that if, when this government appointed a commission to investigate the operations of the Pension Act, they had selected as commissioners a farmer, a blacksmith or a lawyer there would have been a great outcry against the proceeding.

Lake Grain Rates

And why? Because those men would not know anything about the question of pensions.
What about a lawyer?

A lawyer would not know very much about the pension question unless he was directly connected with the Pension Board or acted in some similar capacity. What do we find here? We appoint a commission. I ask hon. members: Who were on that commission who knew anything about rates on the Great Lakes or elsewhere? They make a report. Are we bound to accept a report which comes from people who know as little about freight rates on the Great Lakes or elsewhere in Canada as I do? I know nothing about it. This is a proposition which should be carefully considered.
May I point out that Mr. Symington of Winnipeg who is perhaps one of the greatest rate experts in Canada was solicitor for this commission.

He may have been a fine solicitor. I understand he was not a member of this board. He may have been a solicitor for the board-I do not know. Can the hon. member tell me who was connected with that board who knows anything about shipping rates or transportation?

I have pleasure in answering the question. I am not personally ec-quainted with Mr. McLean who was chairman of the commission but I have read in the papers that he was a very great expert on this matter.

Who told the hon. member that Mr. McLean was an expert on any question of freight rates? He never had any experience in the world. Mr. Thomson, who was a member of this House at one time, a very estimable gentleman, was on the board.
Does the hon. member see the position he is putting the government in just now?
I am not particular about it.
Why should the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) be worried about it? He is altogether too anxious about the government.

It really seems a very strange position that we from this side of the House should be defending the actions of the government, while a member from the other side of the House is condemning the government; but I am not worried.
I am not worrying, my conscience is clear.
A member on the Conservative side is worrying.
I am pointing out the incongruity of it.
I think the hon. member is lacking in a sense of humour.

I appreciate what the leader of the Progressives has said; but I am as independent as he is, when it comes to a question whether I should take a certain stand. I cannot agree with my hon. friend for South York (Mr. Maclean) because his anxiety is shown in this particular connection.
The member for South York was anxious yesterday.

But my hon. friend the
leader of the Progressives must not forget that we on this side of the House are not bound down. We are not slaves to any policy the government may bring down. On this side of the House we sometimes use our common sense and judgment; and I hope, Mr. Chairman, that our judgment is generally correct. If the leader of the Progressives were following this government, he would sit down in a servile manner and support any proposition they might introduce. I think that is his position to-night. But if there is a proposition brought forth which I consider to be unfavourable to Canadian interests, un-Canadian in the extreme, I will oppose it. I did not read very extensively the report of this commission, but I would just as soon take the report of three seamen on grain or freight rates as I would accept the proposition which has been placed before us by this commission. I take the stand-and my friends on the government benches do not like my proposition very much-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Go right ahead.
I do not think they are paying much attention to it.

My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has taken the course which perhaps lets him out rather easily-a constitutional course. I would rather suggest to my hon. friend from Halifax that he should take the common sense of this thing, and let the constitutional aspect be governed more or less by the Minister of Justice, who is always ready and willing to give an opinion, and I think any decision coming from his department is right.

I would ask the government to take into consideration, quietly, calmly and deliberately, the proposition as to whether or not we are going to destroy a Canadian industry which has taken some 15 years to build up, in favour of American industries, and American companies, which to-day are being organized in the various states along the Great Lakes, to the detriment of our Canadian trade. I would think, although not having given very serious thought to the question, that there must be some way of dealing with exorbitant rates on the Great Lakes without throwing into the hands of a foreign government the shipping interests on those lakes. We might have another commission, for example, composed of a fisherman, a blacksmith and a banker, who know nothing about shipping interests on the Great Lakes, who would advise the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to how he could control those rates. I do not think any person can see that I am very antagonistic towards the government, but I for one, as a Canadian, do not like the proposition to throw open an industry which has taken twenty years to establish, which has in a few years increased our grain exports from Montreal from 5,000,000 bushels to
150,000,000 bushels. I do not think we should rush in and give those interests which were opposing us the right to interfere with our lake freight rates, unless we get the same treatment from the United States.
American grain.
This does no injury to Canadian trade. It gives labour to Canadian citizens; it makes revenue for Canadian merchants and shippers, and incidentally the taxes come back in a degree to the government.
Is that coast-wise trade?
No.
Certainly not.

A few days ago when we had under consideration something regarding shipping, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) questioned my statement and asserted that no grain went through the Quebec elevator last year.
No. The statement I made was that last year no boats carrying export grain were diverted from Montreal to Quebec.

As I think Hansard will show, and as my recollection goes, my hon. friend stated that no grain or very little was put through that elevator. I will, however, accept my hon. friend's correction. Last year there was put through the port of Montreal 147,564,328 bushels, and of that quantity, 83,944,389 bushels consisted of United States grain, as against 63,000,000 bushels Canadian grain, or about 20,000,000 bushels less Canadian grain than American grain were put through the port of Montreal. Through the port of Quebec we put a total of 5,968,765 bushels last year. My hon. friend who represents that city in this House, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) tells me that already in the first month of navigation, the elevator at Quebec has put through something over a million bushels. We have had a very reasonable discussion upon this resolution. We have in some regards got away from it-[DOT]
Did the grain that went through the port of Quebec come in by boat or rail?

I have not the information for last year, but I gather that part of it must have gone in by boat. This year it is going in by boat. Last year there were 13,000,000 bushels of United States corn, and corn is always largely shipped to this country by water. This is a better route for corn than the southern route. The corn cools off with the transshipment, and it carries better.
I was proceeding to say that we have had a reasonable discussion upon the resolution, and the bill will come along to-morrow. It is getting late, and while I do not want to stop any further discussion, I would ask that
Lake Grain Rates

if lion, members discuss this resolution, they keep to the question of the resolution, and we *will take up the coasting laws later on.

I should like to say just a word in connection with this resolution. A couple of hon. members asked a question why grain was carried from Canadian ports into American ports more cheaply than it was between two Canadian ports. While I am frank to admit that I know nothing about shipping regulations on the Great Lakes, I know a little about them in Vancouver. I may say that I was interested in some trading steamers on the Pacific coast, and we always gave a better rate into an American port than we did from one Canadian port to another. I will tell you the reason why. We could go into Seattle, for instance, at 6 o'clock in the evening, and we could get discharged and leave at 6 o'clock the next morning We could never get that in a Canadian port. If we went into Victoria at 6 o'clock in the evening, we would have to wait until 8 o'clock the next morning before we started to unload. Time counts, more particularly when you are paying your crews and other expenses. We gave a better rate and we made money by doing so.
A good deal has been said on this side of the House in connection with freight rates I understand that six of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are on the Great Lakes, and I am going to put up a suggestion to the government, namely that this government give the grain commissioners a charter of those six steamers for a dollar each per annum; that they operate them, and that the profit they make on those steamers for the season control the rate that is charged on the Great Lakes, they to put their own crews and their own captains on the ships, and be responsible for the ships. All the government should ask them to do is to pay a dollar each and to cover them with insurance.
The rates will foe twice as high as they are now.
I think the people on the lakes would be perfectly satisfied with the rates that this would establish.

I should like to make a reference or two to some statements that have been made this evening. The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll' seems to question the ability of the commissioners to examine into this question. While, perhaps, it is the prerogative of the government to defend those men, I submit that it is impossible to get men of the same profession or of the same class to examine into a business of this kind. According to the hoi.

Aj
member for South Cape Breton, it would be necessary to have grain shippers themselve.' examine into this matter. Could we get a fair decision from men engaged in grain shipping? According to his argument, if you had a liquor case to investigate, the prosecution would have to have a bootlegger to conduct the investigation. That is the sum and substance of his argument.
As regards the remarks made by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) I think he has not read very carefully the report of the commission, because it conclusively proves that unloading conditions and conditions with regard to return cargoes and everything else were just as favourable at Canadian ports as they were at American ports. The commissioners point that out most conclusively, and state that there was no particular reason whatever for the discrimination. I should like to make just one reference in this respect. They refer particularly to the Standard Shipping Company, which charters or controls, and still does to-day, 54 per cent of the Canadian space on the Great Lakes, and which controls 27 per cent on the American lakes. They make this reference:
It seems clear that competition on the Canadian side is not nearly so keen as on the American side. In fact, among Winnipeg brokers-
That is those who are handling or who have control of all the space on the lakes.
-it is almost non-existent.
That will depend on when the argument is through. If my hon. friend is going to talk all night-
It is through so far as I am concerned, if the minister will give me the information.

I can give my hon. friend no information until the resolution is passed

Canada Shipping Act
Then I shall be prepared to give him the information immediately.

The minister stated that the bill will compel shippers to show the rates, amount of space available, and so on. According to the evidence adduced before the commission, and as I think myself, that would tend to give these men an opportunity of submitting to the government statements similar to those which they have placed be-. fore the commission,-statements advancing their own point of view but entirely out of keeping with the facts as they were proved to exist. These men have deceived us twice: they deceived us when they erected this combine on the lakes, and they deceived, or at least attempted to deceive, the commission which the government appointed to investigate their activities. This notwithstanding, however, the government proposes now to accept their word again in regard to the advertising of rates, and so forth. I am not in the mood now to tolerate that. They burnt us twice, and I think we should be careful now. There is particular mention in the introduction of the reasons that impelled the government to institute a commission to investigate the whole matter, as it applies to western Canada. I am pleased to note that special reference is made to that part of the country, because we feel that we have been oppressed time and time again. We do not want to rehearse the various ways in which we have been harassed, and our products practically stolen from us, but we undoubtedly want the government to do something by way of legislation to prevent these people from taking an unfair advantage of us again. An exhibition should be made of some of these men instead of their word being taken again after they have deceived the community as they have done. Does the minister not think that we have a right to demand other tribunals to show to the government what the facts and the conditions warrant in the way of rates?
Would the hon. member be in favour of the Grain Commission taking over the six steamers the government has on the lakes?

I am reminded that a few moments ago the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) thought that he was rising to the defence of the government. If this legislation is not satisfactory to my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) then he might offer some suggestions as to how it can be improved. When we get into committee he can submit those suggestions; but if hon. gentlemen are disposed to delay the legislation, if they do not want to let it go through, I do not see why we should press it.

No, no.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Robb thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 235 with respect to Freight Rates for the Carriage of Grain by Lake and River Navigation.
When shall the bill be read the second time?
I hope to proceed with the bill either to-morrow or Monday.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to repeal section 958 of the Canada Shipping Act, as enacted by chapter sixty-four of the statutes of 1908, and to enact in lieu thereof that the Governor in Council may, from time to time, by order in council declare that the foregoing provisions of this part shall not, for the period specified in such order in council, apply, either throughout Canada or in any specified waters of Canada, to the ships or vessels, or to any specified, ascertained or ascertainable class or number of the ships or vessels, of any foreign country.
Is it the purpose of the government to suspend the laws in regard to American ships if the American government does not suspend its laws so far as Canadian ships are concerned?

Under the law as it is we have the power to suspend the coastal laws as they affect a foreign country if that country is willing to reciprocate. We are seeking to change the law to give the Governor in Council power in any emergency, if the necessity arises, to suspend the coastal laws for a time in any particular district or in regard to certain vessels. Of course, this power will be exercised with discretion and will be invoked 8nly when it is absolutely necessary. I think we may safely trust the government not to injure Canadian shipping. What we propose to do is intended not for the benefit of American shipping but in the interests of the Dominion, and will be resorted to only to serve that end.

Under what power were the coastal laws suspended last fall, and also by a previous government a few years ago?

Senate and House of Commons

I really am not in a position to answer that question. Under the law as it stands there is certainly nothing to entitle the government to suspend the coastal laws. I understand that in 1913 they were suspended, but only by virtue of an agreement with the companies themselves who submitted without questioning the legality or otherwise of the action. Last year I believe they were suspended only for one or two trips of the season. The government undoubtedly took a chance, because under the law as it stands they have no power in the matter.

I would point out to the
minister that when the coasting laws were suspended the suspension was a dead letter. The chances were that if any ships went into the Bay ports at that time they would never get out again.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all
last session and this session we have heard economy preached in this House not only by one particular group but by all groups. Unfortunately no economy can be practised without hurting somebody; it must stop works which would give employment to people, or less wages must be paid. Yet it would seem that at the rate at which expenditures are increasing and the earning power of a great portion of the people decreasing, something will have to be done in the way of rigid and painful economy. I believe that economy, like charity, should begin at home. Possibly it would hurt the other (fellow less, he who has been practising economy until it does hurt, if we here practised a little economy of our own. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on May 23, 1922, said:
I must to-day present two thoughts which ares of paramount importance. The first is as to the need, the deep and earnest need, of economy. That means that we must appeal both to members of parliament and to the people to pass what I may call self-denying ordinances.
I believe that when the indemnity was increased in 1920 the chief argument in its favour was that the price of everything had gone up. If that argument was good then, it is surely true that the opposite argument is good now, because the cost of living is surely, if slowly, becoming less. Farm products have almost lost their value. I have heard members in this House admit that last

Senate and House of Commons
year they took part of their indemnity to make up the deficiency on their farms. That makes me wonder how the man is getting along who has a farm but no indemnity.
I intend to move an amendment to this clause which will ask members to place upon themselves a self-denying ordinance. If we do this we shall then have much more weight in explaining to our constituents that it is bad policy to ask for what might be called "grab" improvements for any particular constituency. There is no need to dwell upon the severe economic depression through which we are passing. Some believe that we are through the worst of it, and I hope they are right, but at least it can be said that Ontario agriculturists to-day are suffering more acutely than for many years past. I am led to move this amendment because I know a great maDy people have been forced this year to do without telephones and daily pape;, not because they are luxuries, but because they must do without something in order to make their income and their expenses meet.
The real reason however, that I am anxious to amend this clause is that those who are suffering because of the rigid economy which they must practise would be helped in spirit by us here passing upon ourselves a self-denying ordinance. Of late years the impression has gone abroad that members of parliament are more concerned about themselves-which would include their pay-than about anyone else. This is not a desirable condition, and possibly if at great suffering to ourselves we decreased our pay, ultimately this suspicion would be removed and our selfdenial 'would really do a great deal towards putting heart into the people who to-day are suffering.
Now possibly it will be said, or at least it will be thought by a great many members that it is expensive to be a member of parliament, that we are supposed to give to all charitable and all sporting and all literary needs in our constituencies. My own opinion is that generous giving to many things in a constituency is a subtle way of buying popularity. I do not mean by that that we should be robbed of the privilege as individuals of giving where we think we should, but this wholesale sort of giving that one associates with politics and politicians is, I am convinced, bad for the giver and bad for the receiver of the gift. That is one thing on which I took a rigid stand during my campaign. I carefully explained that I would not give to people who came begging for gifts, and I have lived up to that, with I believe no disastrous results either to myself or those
asking for the gifts. It is true that a member of parliament between sessions because of an awakened and interested electorate works much more strenuously now than in days gone by. I think that sort of thing should be increased and encouraged. I for one intend to cover thoroughly as I did last recess my riding, but I do not think the cut which I shall ask at the conclusion of this speech will prevent any member so inclined from meeting his electorate.
I believe that another one of the chief pleas that was put up by the members of the government of 1920 when this' increase was made was that it would do away with the party fund, that if the members were given $4,000 a year they would not be slaves to the party nor to the party fund. The best proof that that is not true is the voting as we have witnessed it in this House. Then is it asking too much-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A point of order was raised that the hon. member for Southeast Grey had made a statement which reflects upon the independence of the members of the House of Commons and upon their integrity. That particular point is under discussion; that is the point of order.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I desire to say one word upon the point of order. If I understood the hon. member for Southeast Grey correctly, in the course of her remarks she made the statement that one of the reasons why the sessional indemnity had been increased in the year 1920 was the fact that it would do away with what is commonly known as an election fund, and she proceeded to base her statement upon a remark made in 1920 by the present Speaker of this House. Up to that point there was certainly no infringement of the. rules of order. But the hon. member for Southeast Grey proceeded immediately afterwards to say that the increase of the indemnity did not have this effect as was proven by the votes given in the House at the present time. That is the statement complained of. If that statement means anything, it means that hon. members of this House owing to the fact that they have received campaign funds, or that they expect to receive campaign funds from some source, vote according to the dictates of the sources from which these funds are supplied. There can be no other interpretation to these words. I respectfully submit that under the ordinary rules and usages of parliament, it is forbidden for any hon. member to cast a reflection upon the honour and integrity of any individual member, or upon the honour or integrity of the House as a whole. If a reflection has not been cast upon an individual member, it certainly has been cast upon the integrity of the House as a whole, and for that reason the words should be retracted. If not retracted the hon. member for Southeast Grey should at least explain to the House that such was not the significance that she desired to give to the words that were uttered.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member who has just spoken how he applies his present position and argument to the charges that have been frequently made in this House, according to my recollection, that the government or a certain party has been assisted into power, so to speak, by certain large financial interests. We have heard these charges commonly. I should therefore like to know how the particular point of order applies to cases like that?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I may be allowed to reply to my hon. friend without departing from the point of order. The answer is very easy to give. In the one case, certain interests are accused of having elected members to this House and the accusation is levelled at some person or persons outside of the House. In

Senate and Home oj Commons
this particular instance, the members of this House are accused of voting in order to please those interests. There is a great difference between the two cases.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I want to raise the point as to whether the remark in question is a reflection upon the honour of any member of this House, because I have heard it seriously contended that it is the duty of members who associate themselves with a' party to vote according to the views of that party-

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: and for the reason that they are supported in this House by the party caucus. I am saying that quite seriously. That is seriously contended by those who argue against group government. And so 1 would say there is no direct onslaught upon the honour of any member of this House by the general reflection just made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I think it is stretching the point a little too far to say that is an attack upon the honour of any member of this House.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I should like to point out that the hon. member for Southeast Grey qualified her remark. She stated definitely that she had no intention of reflecting on the integrity of any members of the House. That is a sufficient qualification and retraction of what she said before. As it has been customary to accept such a statement as a retraction I think we ought to pursue that course in her case as well as in others.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I will withdraw the statement if it is unparliamentary and beg everybody's pardon. The thing I want to say, if I may be allowed to do so, is this: When some of the good party men have declared their views outside on certain questions and we see them come in and vote u the opposite way what are we to think? Let me continue with the quotation of what the present Speaker of the House said in his speech upon the increase in the indemnity He said:
A party gets funds to elect its candidates, the men who contribute to that party fund expect the member elected in return for the aid received, will do the bidding of those who have paid the election expenses. Sir, I am right in saying that with the increased indemnities, the party fund will be a thing of the past, and if for no other reason the people of Canada would approve the action of parliament in this regard.
Recalling the argument that was advanced in 1920 for the increase in the indemnity, an argument in the very opposite direction can be made now in favour of a decrease. I believe that out of sympathy for the people

in general because of the severe economi" depression through which we are passing- we should do all we can to help and if we practise economy we will do much to strengthen the morale of the people and make them feel that we are indeed their servants and their brothers. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) that the words " four thousand " as they appear in section 32 be struck out and that the words " three thousand five hundred" be substituted therefor.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I might be permitted to make a few observations I should like to say that in 1920 I voted for the increased indemnity and I am prepared now to vote against this amendment. Furthermore, if I had a seconder I should be inclined to move an amendment providing that the indemnity should be So,.000 instead of $4,000 and I think the majority of the House would support me.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Especially those who
have many children.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well it may come to that. I was under the impression in 1920 that members of parliament should be pai l a reasonable indemnity to permit them to discharge their duties in a satisfactory manner and to give all time necessary to the affairs of this country. I think that by giving a fair indemnity, by paying a reasonable amount, men who are qualified in every way will be attracted to the service of their country. If that is not done professional or business men will not be induced to abandon *heir profession or their business, sometimes for eight months in the year, to attend to the affairs of the people in this House.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What about the children?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I will leave the answer to my hon. friend. It is well enough for any hon. member who has not very many obligations, who does not keep up a house in his own locality, or maintain a large family, to say that an indemnity of $2,000 a year is quite enough. It may be quite enough, and probably too much for some of those hon. members; but for anyone who has to leave his business for a certain period and keep up his household and family, and come here to Ottawa and remain for a few months under double expense, I think $4,000 is really too little under the circumstances. If the members of this House were well paid, I think it would be the means of attracting the best qualified men of the country to the House to represent the people of their districts.

Senate and House of Commons

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I feel that something ought to be said in regard to this amendment. I have been in this House, as many other members have, for a great many years. I have witnessed from time to time resolutions of this kind moved with variant motives for a reduction of the indemnity paid to members. I happen to be in, perhaps, a fortunate position to-night, as far as I am personally concerned because, before the last election and subsequent to the increased indemnity, I was publicly asked, before an audience in Vancouver of perhaps two or three thousand citizens, my reasons for supporting the increased indemnity I answered the question as briefly as I could in such words as this, that if the electors of Vancouver did not consider that my services as a representative of that city were worth $4,000 the proper course would be to vote against me and leave me at home. I returned to this House with a majority of some 5,000 votes, which I consider at least vindicates my personal position in this matter.
I want to say something further, not perhaps so personal. I am inclined to think, Mr. Chairman, that if I attended the House not too assiduously, if I were present in my seat half of the time, if I did not give that attention to the matters coming before the House which I considered they certainly merited, and my conscience was still alive, I might hesitate to accept the full indemnity. I am not constituting myself a judge of the action of any member. It may be that some members do not give close attention to their duty. It is not my purpose or duty to judge of them. I am responsible for my own action, but I will say this with all the emphasis of which I am capable: that when I leave my home and family, maintain that home on the Pacific coast and live in Ottawa for approximately six months-and I think it will be fully six months by the .time I get back to my home again-and attend to these duties as assiduously as I can, an indemnity of $4,000 a year is certainly not too much. There are members who have few responsibilities, or perhaps no responsibility, no family connections, no particular expenditure in maintaining a house, and no losses in business. They are happy and fortunate, from a monetary standpoint perhaps, and ahead of the game. If such a member feels that the indemnity under those circumstances is altogether too high, the remedy is very simple. Let him return to the coffers, as has been done by individual members, that portion of the indemnity which he feels he is not entitled to take. But I do wish to say that a member fortunately, or I think perhaps unfortunately, placed in that position, who has no responsibility or no
ties of this kind, should not constitute himself a judge of what is due to those who certainly lose and lose heavily.	[DOT]
It might be advisable to say this-and I think I will be acquitted of any censoriousness in saying it-that a member should attend the sessions of this House closely and assiduously, should be. in his seat regularly, sometimes perhaps for very long hours, should attend the committee work of the House and the variant duties which devolve upon a member of parliament in this country, and during the recess should give careful attention to the public welfare. If he does that, there is not too much in the indemnity for the services rendered:	Furthermore I do not
think the people of Canada begrudge any member of parliament who gives conscientious attention to his duties along these lines the indemnity which members have been drawing. Of course we all know perfectly well that there is a certain amount of glamour surrounding the so-called sacrifice of boldly moving in the House for the voluntary reduction of the indemnity, when that is positively or practically safeguarded by a general committal of the House to the indemnity before the question is brought up. That is a situation which has arisen in the past, and sometimes does present itself; but I do not appreciate very highly the action based on conditions and circumstances of that kind. It is not usual for a bill of this kind to be introduced in the House until it has been considered carefully by a committee, and until there has been knowledge of it, and an opportunity of expression of opinion, so that there may be reasonable unanimity; and that is a reasonable proposition. Under cover of that known unanimity or approximate unanimity, occasionally there are those who will say: So far as I am concerned I do not intend to accept this indemnity and I move for its reduction. I cannot very highly appreciate that course of action. Perhaps I have spoken plainly, but I do think when we are discussing a matter of this kind it is desirable to be very frank and very plain as to the position that we take.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not wish to shirk stating my opinion upon this matter. I should like, in commencing, to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) for her sincerity of purpose and for the absolutely honesty of the attempt that she is making at the present time to reduce the indemnity. I do not know for a certainty, but I am credibly informed that she returned $1,500 of her salary last year-I may be wrong, but I think that was correct-and that is a

Senate and House of Commons
very good proof that she is quite in earnest in the move that she is making.
Mr. DUF*F: She can do that again this year.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is so. Still, every member has a right to his or her opinions, and probably the moral effect may be worth thinking about if some sacrifice is attached to the action. I do not believe for one moment that the thing has been done for any spectacular effect. I am perfectly convinced that the action is sincere and honest right through.
As regards the amount, I cannot support the amendment. I know my own circumstances. I have rather a large farm; I have no boys of my own, and I have four hired men engaged there at the present time running my farm. I shall be away for nearly six months, and anyone who knows about conditions, knows exactly what it means to neglect the business for that time. I know what the expense of keeping a house in Ottawa is, and the expense of keeping a house in Manitoba and running back there. I am perfectly satisfied that I for one could not be in public life if the salary is going to 'be reduced very much lower than it is at the present time. I state that opinion sincerely, and I am quite prepared to take the verdict of my people a', home. I am speaking simply because I want to place myself on record. I believe that members should conscientiously try to do their duty in the House; that they ought to giye serious consideration to all questions that come up; that they should take t.heir duty seriously. We are here in the parliament of Canada, and our actions have a tremendous effect for good or evil throughout this Dominion. Although not taking a very large part in the work of the House at times, I feel the responsibility of every act that we take, and I think, perhaps, the country will not begrudge us the salary of $4,000. In conclusion, let me say again, because I want to emphasize this, that I sincerely believe in the honesty of motive and purpose of the hon. member for Southeast Grey.

Mr. Chairman, if you can hear my voice above the din of conversation, I should be glad to make a few remarks with regard to this clause, clause 3 of the bill dealing with section 35 of the original act. If hon. members will look at the act as it originally was,

The effect of the bill now introduced will be to relieve the members of that restriction. It is indeed significant that such a proposal should be brought to this House at this time. I would ask you, Sir: If there happened to be a provincial election in British Columbia or in Alberta and members from those provinces were to press for such a proposal as this, would it meet with the general approval of members of this House, or if it did, would it meet with the approval of the people of this country? Of the latter, there is no doubt in my mind. Their rejection of a proposal of that kind would probably be very loudly voiced. During the last two weeks of the last session, which is the only one excepting this one that I have had the privilege of being in this House, and during any other sessions of which hon. members have spoken to me, it appears almost a certainty, a constant happening, that during those two weeks there comes up the greatest bulk of the most important legislation. When that restriction was formerly introduced into the act, it was for the purpose of keeping members here who might otherwise be anxious to go on a holiday or to go home on business.

Mr. Chairman, with your kind permission, I wish to say a few words regarding the question under

Senate and House oj Commons
discussion. My impression was that a number of members would give their views on the reduction of the parliamentary indemnity, because at the opening session of this Parliament, I was requested by a number of the Progressive party to give my opinion on this matter. They wanted me again to bring up the question; however, my answer was that I would support them if they would follow the course that I had taken.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that, in 1920, when the increase of the parliamentary indemnity was moved by Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister, he had stated in this House, on the 23rd of June, that he could not meet the wish of hon. gentlemen owing to there being too many pressing needs in behalf of the returned soldier and too many public works to be carried on in the country. A caucus took place on the following day, that is the 24th.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A Liberal or Conservative caucus?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
A Tory or rather a
Unionist caucus. I was not present, however, it was rumoured that a revolt had broken out to the effect that should the Prime Minister not acquiesce to the wish of his party a strike would be called in the workshop. He had already been threatened with such a fate a few weeks previous because the Unionist party of the day had seen its majority of 71 dwindle down to 5. It was therefore agreed at that caucus to increase the parliamentary indemnity. The following day, on the 25th, a bill to that effect was brought down and the parliamentary indemnity was increased to S4,000 per year. At that time, I made my position clear: I moved an amendment against the parliamentary increase, not however, that I thought at the time no more than I do to-day that $4,000 was too much for the members to receive as an indemnity, but to me, it was a question of principle, I would not accept that amount from the hands of the master of the day, because I was fully aware that ho would not be long at the head of the affairs of this country. This is the reason, I was the strongest opponent of the measure. We had at that time, as we have to-day a great deal of war expenditures; we had purchased a number of railways and I foresaw that once this increase was granted it would be difficult to remedy it. The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) must have noticed it even to-day by the behaviour of those who induced her to propose that amendment when this measure
was first introduced, I made up my mind to strongly oppose this increase of indemnity, and, should it be voted, to abstain from applying it to my own pecuniary advantage. My views in the meantime, have not changed. If the hon. members opposite me were sincere-especially those from Ontario as I am informed-when they proclaimed to the people, in 1921, that it was not worth more than $2,500 to be a member at Ottawa; if they were sincere at that time, they must necessarily be now, as I am, and if they always believe that this increase of $1,500 should never have been granted, why do they not distribute it to their electors as I have twice done. They must not pose to-day as champions of economy, preach against this increase and at the same time pocket the money for their personal benefit. That is why I thought it appropriate to make a few remarks. I insist on it, my views have not changed any and when I gave my word to this House that I would not benefit by this increase, I kept my word. I state in all frankness that I did not profit from such an increase. It has cost me $3,000 and I am not complaining over it.

In order to expedite the
business of the House-because no one is more anxious to get home than I am, although I am prepared to carry out my duties to the fullest extent-I shall bring my remarks to a close, especially in view of the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite are apparently determined to obstruct me. I simply wish to declare myself opposed to any attempt to remove the restrictions with regard to the last fifteen days of the session of parliament.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Before the motion is carried I think a word should be said in answer to my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) who, I am sure, was sincere in the remarks he made concerning the removal of the special restrictions applied to the last fifteen days of a session. I must point out, and I should like the press and the country as well as the House of Commons to understand, that the present bill has not for its object the giving of any permission to hon. members to leave the House during the last fifteen days any more than at any other time during the ses-

Senate and House oj Commons
sion. If any hon. member is absent from the House for more than fifteen days during the session he is penalized to the extent of $25 for every day beyond the fifteen, whether the absence occurs at the beginning or during the latter part of the session. I am prepared to admit that much important legislation is introduced during the last days of the session but I also maintain that very many important measures are introduced during the first weeks. The budget speech and tariff resolutions, for instance, generally come before the last two weeks of the session, and there is nothing more important than the budget. The hon. member says that we should remain during the last weeks. I say we should remain all the time. The government cannot be blamed for the date or period when legislation is introduced. There is no desire on the part of the government to leave important legislation until the dying days of the session. This is due to the natural trend of events. Measures are submitted and sent to committees, and engage their attention during nearly the entire session, and it is only after the committees have reported to the House that such measures can be finally dealt with. I maintain that it is just as important for members to be present while those measures are being considered by committees before presentation to the House as when they go through the final stages in the House itself.
Apart from that, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) says that this legislation should not be amended as proposed owing to the fact that certain members are now absent taking part in a provincial election. And he asks: What would be said if a provincial election were being held in Alberta and we were to leave the House to take part in it?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I suggested that in the event of a provincial election being held in Alberta, and we pressed for such an amendment, we might be criticized.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I was just coming to that. He suggested that if in order to take part in such an election he pressed for this amendment, he might be blamed. I respectfully submit to the House that his electors are really the persons to say whether an hon. member should take part in a provincial election or not. The result of a provincial election may be very vital to the welfare of his particular riding, and his electors will seldom blame him for not attending to his duties in the House of Commons at that time. If the electors in the various constituencies where federal members are taking part in the provincial elections-and are therefore in their own way looking after the interests of their constituents-think it would be better for their representatives to remain in the House of Commons, they have their redress, they can vote against those members in the next election and so punish them. But it will be found that in every instance where a provincial election does take place, the electors are keenly disappointed if the federal member takes no part in it but remains at Ottawa to draw his indemnity. Furthermore, a provincial election might take place at some other stage of the session, and under the law as it now stands upon the statute book hon. members could be absent for fifteen days to take part in that election and would not be fined if they were regular in their attendance during the rest of the session.
But there is another view to take. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) in suggesting an amendment which we were glad to accept and incorporate in the bill, stated that if a session lasted for fifty days or over, and some hon. members were absent during the first fifty days, it would be necessary to keep the House in session for another fifteen days in order that they might draw their full indemnity. In the present instance if some hon. members desired to allow their colleagues to take part in the provincial elections in Ontario or in any other province at any other time, they could certainly block legislation for fifteen days to enable those members to come back and escape being fined for their fifteen days' absence. The result would be to put the country to extra expense and nothing would be gained. I respectfully submit to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the committee that when this matter was discussed by the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate there was no desire to relieve any hon. member from attendance in this House. The desire was to make the rule fair, just and equitable for all members at all times during a session. We felt, as I have already explained, that if an hon. member was called away for some reason of urgent public importance in his constituency or for legitimate family reasons during the latter part of a session, he should be treated absolutely the same as the hon. member who happened to be called away for similar reasons during an earlier period of the session.
There is no doubt that when the law was amended in 1920 it was done hastily. If I remember rightly the hon. leader of the party then in power declared in the House about two weeks before the law was amended that there would be no amendment and that the indemnity would not be increased. Pressure

Senate and House oj Commons
was brought to bear upon him and he became convinced by the arguments of his supporters -and I say this with no intention of disparaging the hon. gentleman-that the indemnity should be raised to $4,000. Thereupon legislation was hastily prepared and introduced for the purpose of making the rules more rigid. We have carried out that intention in the present amending act. We have fixed the duration of a session at sixty-five days instead of thirty before any member of this House can draw his full indemnity of $4,000. We have also increased the attendance of the individual member from thirty to fifty days. In spite of the lengthy sessions we have not sought to increase the days of absence although the question was raised in the committee and we have been requested by some hon. members to increase the number of days during which a member could be 1 a.m. absent without sacrificing any part of his indemnity. We did not think such a change would be in the interests of the country. The fine for absence has been increased from $15 to $25 a day. I want once more to make it perfectly clear that this legislation does not give wholesale permission to members to be absent during the last fifteen days but only treats those days on the same basis as all the other days of the session which are equally important.

Mr. STEVENS (for Mr. Black, Yukon) moved the second reading of Bill No. 44, to amend the Yukon Act.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure) in the chair.
On section 1-Recovery or defining of claims, mining property or mineral locations.

I will briefly explain this bill and in doing so I wish to expressly thank the Minister of Justice for his courtesy in permitting it to come up. This is a somewhat technical and formal amendment to the Yukon Act. The Yukon Act, as originally drafted, provided for trials, and so forth, but did not include provision for jury trials in certain cases. The reason for it was this: When Yukon was first opened up and this act was originally passed it was in the days of what was known as "the stampede." Conditions there were in an exceedingly disturbed state, and it was felt that it was not desirable to place such cases as mineral claims and disputes under jury trial as was the case in all other provinces. That condition has long since passed, twenty years ago or nearly so, and to-day Yukon is just as settled and as sober 

shall I say?-in its thought and in its administration as any other part of Canada. All the feverish excitement has long since passed.	This is simply to give to Yukon
rights which are enjoyed by the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have an amendment to offer to this section. The first clause provides for an appeal on interlocutory and final judgments in mining property cases. I do not think it would be advisable to permit appeals on interlocutory judgment; we should limit the appeal to final judgments. I therefore propose to amend the clause so that it will read:
1.	Section forty-six of the Yukon Act, chapter sixty-three of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1908, as enacted by section two of chapter fifty-six of the statutes of 1912, is amended by adding at the end of subsection two thereof the following:-"or if the action be for the recovery of a claim, mining property, mineral claim or location, as defined by the Yukon Placer Mining Act, chapter sixty-four of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, or by the regulations for 'the disposal of quartz mining claims on Dominion lands in the Yukon territory, or of any interest therein or to establish title thereto, or for the definition of or establishment of the boundaries of any such claim, mining property, mineral claim or location, or to establish the right of a claimant to any such claim, raining property, mineral claim or location or interest therein, or to have included within said claim, mining property, mineral claim or location, any land or property, or if the action be for divorce or judicial separation.

Yukon Act

This will give an appeal in mining property cases for final judgments only.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
